player.seasonOutlook: Tucker's cumulative 2025 numbers don't remotely do justice to his immense raw talent. Breaking it down by halves, he hit .291/.395/.537 with 17 homers and 20 steals through the season's first three months, which is top 10 in fantasy valuation in both points-based and rotisserie scoring. He then cratered to .225/.348/.342 rates with just five homers and five steals over the final three months, placing outside the top 190 players overall. Following the season, Tucker revealed that he had been playing through a hand fracture suffered in early June, an explanation that affords promise of a complete rebound from him following the winter's rest. The Dodgers are clearly banking on that, granting him the second-highest contract average annual value of any player in history, while placing him in the heart of a loaded lineup. Anticipate Tucker bouncing back and consider him a first rounder still.

Finally beyond the injury issues that plagued him for much of his first six MLB seasons, Tatis delivered the most well rounded year of his career to date. Though he posted the lowest HR rate of his career (3.6%, resulting in a total of just 25 taters), he vastly improved his contact and his patience at the plate, setting personal bests with his 73.0% contact and 24.1% chase rates. The result was more fantasy points (439) than Tatis scored in 2021 (422), when he hit 42 home runs, and it sets him up for potentially greater things in 2026 as a 27-year-old. He's not without injury risk based upon his track record, but with his skills now making him nearly as strong a pick in points-based as rotisserie leagues, he's a legitimate building block player for fantasy purposes.

After missing only eight games from 2021 to 2023, Riley played just 110 in 2024 and 102 last season, dealing with a fluke broken hand two years ago and three IL visits for core issues last year. His sports hernia surgery in August should help him re-establish his reliability. Even through the injuries, Riley maintained near-elite exit velocity, barrel rate and hard-hit numbers. However, after slightly improving his strikeout rate from 2021-23, he gave back those gains last year, posting his worst rate since his rookie season. It was likely more a matter of his timing being affected by the injury-driven absences than a change in approach. The market is not quite as bullish as in prior years, but at a thin position full of uncertainty, Riley stands out as a risk worth taking.

Devers has been a star since he hit the scene in 2017, but 2025 saw him come to a career crossroads due to an unwillingness to make a much-needed defensive change which ultimately led to him being traded from Boston midseason. The turmoil began in camp and carried over to the regular season when Devers began the season 2-for-27 with 15 strikeouts. He recovered nicely and went onto hit .289/.416/.528 before the infighting became too much and he was sent to San Francisco. The move to Oracle Park and the National League had an impact on his numbers as he hit .236/.347/.480 the rest of the season, but with 20 of his 35 homers after the trade. By season's end, the counting category production was where it should have been even as his average suffered. The now 1B/DH is still an early-round selection.

A model of consistency, durability and elevated floors among pitchers, Valdez hit a rough patch over 2025's final two months, which could explain why he lingered on the free agent market for so long. A .330 BABIP and 60.8 LOB% hinted that his 6.05 ERA during that time was more mirage than trend, while the left-hander's 83 quality starts, 767 2/3 innings pitched and 1,659 fantasy points from 2022-25 combined (all of which ranked top-three at his position) provide fairer perspective on his skills. As an extreme ground baller, Valdez's only team-influenced effect would be the infield defense behind him. The Tigers’ group is strong enough to assure him another potential top-15 fantasy starter stat line.

Amidst a teardown in Minnesota, Ryan stood tall with a career-best 3.42 ERA over a career-high 171 innings in 2025. The right-hander was one of two Twins All-Stars, along with Byron Buxton. Ryan has emerged as one of the team's top starters over the last few seasons, though he could be on his way out in due time as the organization continues to rebuild. Ryan would be befitting of the ace label almost anywhere given that he ranks seventh among qualified starters in strikeout-minus-walk percentage over the last three seasons. Home runs and occasional injuries have held him back from reaching true greatness, but Ryan is only 29 and his best years may still be ahead of him. With six pitches and pinpoint control, Ryan can be drafted with confidence as an SP2 for fantasy leagues.

Bradish underwent Tommy John surgery with an internal brace in June 2024 but returned to start six games down the stretch. While command and control can lag after surgery, he showed little rust, striking out 47 batters against just 10 walks over 32 innings, with velocity in line with his healthy years. The performance was encouraging, but he has totaled only 104.2 innings across the majors and minors over the past two seasons. That likely points to workload management ahead, and expecting him to sustain last season's pace, even if it mirrors his healthy 2023, may be optimistic. A cautious approach is warranted.

Altuve posted a 113 wRC+, his lowest mark in a full season since 2013. While his home-run output climbed to its highest level since 2022, his batting average dipped to a career low outside of the abbreviated 2020 season. A decade ago, that might have been written off as variance, but entering his age-36 season, it may instead point toward the early stages of decline. If that is the case, erosion can accelerate quickly, introducing more risk into a profile that has been remarkably stable for years. Altuve compensated for a modest drop in barrel rate by pulling more flyballs, though there is no guarantee that adjustment sticks. With age, the downside scenarios begin to outweigh the upside, but that reality is typically reflected in the draft cost, and his dual eligibility at second base and outfield still provides some appeal.

Albies had a season to forget in 2025 with a career-low .671 OPS across 157 games with Atlanta. Adding injury to insult, Albies suffered a hamate bone fracture in his left hand during the final week. He is expected to be fully recovered in time for spring training, but the second baseman's inconsistency in recent years makes him tough to trust entering 2026. Historically, Albies has done a disproportionate amount of his damage from the right side of the plate -- his struggles from the left side have led to calls for him to give up switch hitting. An All-Star as recently as 2023, Albies has shown little in recent years to justify enduring optimism, though at least the downward trends have not yet extended to his overall strikeout rate. Further, the 29-year-old still provides efficiency on the basepaths.

Shaky control and a knee injury sustained during a game of Hacky Sack ruined Uribe's 2024, which began with the promise of potential save chances (including in four of the team's first six games). He'd settle for a middle relief role to begin 2025, from which he was every bit as excellent as he was across the final three months of his 2023 debut campaign. Uribe led the league in holds (37) and was third among relievers in both ERA and hard-hit rate allowed. Plus, he managed six saves and a 1.89 ERA in 18 games between the regular season and postseason after stepping back into the closer role for an injured Trevor Megill. That breakthrough puts Uribe in direct competition with Megill for the team's ninth-inning role this season, with your league's inclusion of saves or holds ultimately determining Uribe's value. He'll be one of the best closers or holds-getters, however it shakes out.

One of the unluckiest pitchers of 2025, with a league-high .362 BABIP, and the second widest ERA-FIP differential in the wrong direction, among qualified relievers, Jax could be one of the position's biggest sleepers with some correction in those departments. Combine his past two seasons and he has the third best K/BB ratio (5.49), fourth-best FIP (2.21), and 62 saves plus holds (18th among relievers), underscoring his elite skill set. As spring training dawns, the Rays don't have a clear closer, a role from which Jax could be a top-10 positional fantasy option if they shift off their longstanding tendency to �mix and match� out of the bullpen. He'll be a top source of holds or saves nevertheless, making him one of the top relievers to target once the clear, elite closers are off the board.

Sheehan's return from May 2024 Tommy John surgery couldn't have gone much more smoothly, especially since he returned to big-league action in only 13 months. From July 6 forward, he scored 185 fantasy points, 17th among pitchers, while posting encouraging 30.6% strikeout and 7.6% walk rates that represented a definite step forward from his 2023 numbers. Sheehan was considered one of the better pitching prospects before the injury, so he should take another step forward, particularly in terms of volume, in 2026. The Dodgers might keep him on an innings cap, with 130-140 being a good guess, but that's plenty for him to warrant mid-round consideration in fantasy leagues.

Just about everything that could possibly have gone wrong for Rutschman in 2025, his age-27 season, did. He hit just .203/.300/.332 across the first two months, made trips to the IL for both obliques (left in June, right in August) and was ultimately pressed for his job by top prospect Samuel Basallo. That competition is the biggest lingering issue, as both players appear likely to make the team in a catcher/DH combination for a team that has a lot of other DH alternatives. Rutschman was previously a budding points-league star thanks to his well-rounded offensive game and the promise of hefty DH time. With that no longer a guarantee, he needs a standout spring to rekindle a top-5 positional valuation in the format. That ceiling remains possible, considering his age and skill set, however.

One of the league's best young power/speed threats, De La Cruz was one of only five players with as many as 50 home runs and 75 steals between the date of his MLB debut (June 6, 2023) and the end of last July -- and the only one with as many as 100 steals over that stretch. Unfortunately, he struggled mightily over the season's final two months, batting just .221/.280/.341 with three homers and eight steals (in 10 attempts) over 52 games, likely as a result of his playing through a partially torn quadriceps. The winter's rest should afford De La Cruz time to sufficiently heal, but his funk served as a reminder that his free-swinging nature at the plate deepens his statistical downside, not to mention is significantly more useful in rotisserie than points-based leagues. To that point, he finished 17th on the 2024 Player Rater, but only 50th in fantasy points scored, so keep that disparity in mind as you weigh your investment in a rebound.

People might call him Mr. Smile, but around these parts, we like to call him Mr. Consistency. Lindor has averaged 32 home runs and 30 stolen bases for the past three seasons and, had he stolen one more base in 2024, he'd have joined Barry Bonds (1995-97) as the only players to go 30/30 in three straight years. Lindor's underlying metrics took a slight step backwards last season, hardly shocking from a then-31-year-old, but that's countered by his being one of the game's most durable players, averaging 158 games the past four seasons. If there's any knock on him, it's that he has a history of somewhat slow starts, his first-half career OPS being 57 points lower than in the second half. Lindor is also questionable for Opening Day following hamate bone surgery in February, which could also extend his tendency for sluggish Aprils. No matter, as if his top-20 overall draft stock isn't to your liking (but it should be!), simply jot down his drafting manager's cell phone number and remember to make a trade-inquiry call around May 15.

Machado authored his seventh All-Star campaign in 2025, winning the Silver Slugger with 27 homers and 95 RBI across 159 games with the Padres during the regular season. The third baseman has fallen just shy of 30 homers the last two years, and his OPS has been under .800 three years running, showing a decreased but still highly respectable performance baseline. At 33 years old, Machado is not much of a runner -- he's grounded into a whopping 41 double plays over the past two seasons -- though he can still chip in a fair number of stolen bases thanks mostly to his veteran instincts. There is still a lot to like here, including durability at a position that sees a sudden drop-off in quality deeper in the player pool.

Fully recovered from June 2023 Tommy John surgery, deGrom in 2025 made more starts (30) and pitched more innings (172 2/3) than he had in any season since his back-to-back Cy Young seasons of 2018-19, remarkably doing so at the age of 37. He exhibited similarly elite average fastball velocity (97.5 mph) and whiff rate on his slider (39.0%), yet couldn't match the lofty strikeout rates, to those prime years. That's not unexpected from a pitcher at deGrom's age, and injury setbacks will remain a worry for the remainder of his career. An extreme fly-ball lean over his final 10 starts (an MLB-leading 42.1%) also heightens regression concerns. He still has what it takes to be a fantasy ace, but the steep downside present in his profile also makes him a dicey leading-man pick.

A dominating ninth-inning force in Minnesota for 3.5 seasons, Duran's career truly took off following his deadline deal to the Phillies last July. Finally bestowed with a ninth-inning role all his own, the right-hander saved an MLB-leading 16 games for his new team, all the while maintaining his top-shelf, closer-caliber raw stuff. Duran returns in the same role for a competitive 2026 Phillies team, giving him a legitimate chance to contend for the fantasy points/Player Rater lead at his position. His combination of a 100-plus-mph fastball and whiff-generating knuckle curve make him one of the most attractive relief pitchers in drafts.

Yelich's 644 plate appearances last season marked his highest total since 2022, while his 29 home runs were his most since 2019. He wasn't quite able to reach 20 steals for a third straight season but was still productive on the basepaths with 16 thefts. He topped 100 RBI for just the second time in his career and finished with a .264/.343/.452 slash line in 150 games. Yelich saw more action than ever at designated hitter with just 19 appearances in the outfield -- which could limit his positional eligibility in 2026 -- and that's unlikely to change much going forward given the back issues he's dealt with throughout his time in Milwaukee. Now entering his age-34 season, Yelich's swing should continue to age well, but some modest regression wouldn't be surprising at this point in his career.

The fireballer put together his best season ever at age 37, successfully converting 32 of 34 save chances for the Red Sox during the regular season with a career-low 1.17 ERA. Chapman was virtually untouchable in the ninth inning with his trademark fastball and nasty breaking pitch. Shockingly, he cut his walk rate down to a career-low mark of 6.6 percent after being at or above 15 percent each of the prior four seasons. It was the dramatic reversal in that particular department that fueled his renaissance, though it's understandable to be skeptical given his history of control woes. Signed to an extension last August, Chapman will return to the closer role to which he is highly accustomed and attempt to continue bucking historical trends with his dominance at an advanced age.

Diaz took advantage of his home digs in 2025, hitting 18 of his career-high 25 homers at Steinbrenner Field. He was no slouch on the road with a .780 OPS, but the Rays' move back to Tropicana Field in 2026 looms large as Diaz has 37 homers in 338 career games at the Trop. While he may not have standout power, he has tapped into more in recent years, enough to supplement his high batting average and make Diaz a fantasy standout if not quite a superstar. Primarily a DH at this stage, Diaz retains first-base eligibility for at least one more season, and a case can be made that he's underrated among the wider drafting public. Expect him to continue batting in the top third of the order every single day in his age-34 season.

One of 2025's biggest disappointments, Williams simply couldn't get the job done in the ninth for the Yankees. It took him just one month to get removed as their closer, after he surrendered as many earned runs in that time (10) as he had during the entirety of his career-year 2023. His season-ending ERA wound up being nearly three full runs higher than the total over his first six MLB seasons. In Williams' strong defense, however, he had outrageous numbers over the final four months in terms of batting average allowed (.172) and strikeout rate (38.6%) -- and he was done in by a 55.2 LOB% that was lower than any qualified reliever had posted in three years. The Mets, who signed him to serve as their 2026 closer, surely saw this and expect a full rebound. We tend to agree.

For only the second time in his nine MLB seasons, Pagan seized hold of a closer opportunity and thrived in it, this time setting personal bests with his 56 games finished, 32 saves and 340 fantasy points (eight more than in his other closer year of 2019). A much-improved splitter had a lot to do with it, fueling career bests of a .161 BAA and .507 OPS allowed to lefties. That should ensure Pagan a long ninth-inning leash, though he's one of the greater risk/reward closers based upon his skill set, as an extreme fly baller whose control is only so-so. Draft Pagan in the middle rounds, once the higher-ceiling closers are gone.

A ruptured quadriceps tendon prematurely ended what was an otherwise excellent year for Adam in setup relief, as he turned in a second straight year of a sub-2.00 ERA and at least 25 holds and 70 strikeouts in 2025. Keep tabs on his health once spring training opens. When healthy, he’ll almost assuredly serve as Mason Miller’s primary setup man and fantasy insurance policy. Adam’s skill set is top-20 caliber among relief pitchers, so expect a return to that form sometime before midseason at the latest.

By a show of hands, who had Pages finishing with the second-most home runs on the Dodgers, trailing only Shohei Ohtani? Exactly. Pages provided stability for a roster dealing with injuries throughout the season, appearing in 156 games, mostly in center field, while showing off one of the strongest outfield arms in the league. Pages' chase rate is elevated, but he struck out at a near-league-average rate last season, suggesting improved swing decisions could allow him to rely less on pulled flyballs and more on hitting the ball with greater authority. Stolen-base efficiency remains a concern, as Pages was caught seven times in 21 attempts, and continued issues could earn him the red light.

Doyle broke out in 2024 with 23 homers, 30 steals and a .763 OPS during his second MLB campaign, but he regressed significantly last season with a .233/.274/.376 slash line in 138 contests. He still provided some power and speed production with 15 long balls and 18 stolen bases, but his run production was lacking with 57 RBI and 57 runs. He made strong contact at a similar clip to 2024 with a 44.6 hard-hit rate, which provides hope for a rebound in 2026 despite the down campaign. Doyle's elite defense in center field will help him to maintain a regular spot in the lineup, and his decent floor in homers and steals make him a bounce-back candidate with a solid floor despite a poor surrounding lineup.

At casual glance, Pepiot's 2025 has the guise of �spinning his wheels� or worse, a small step backwards. His ERA rose by more than a quarter of a run, he averaged 0.1 fewer fantasy points per start, and he whiffed only 24.6% of the hitters he faced after 26.3% the year before. Make no mistake, however, that the Rays' return to Tropicana Field for 2026 is a huge positive for Pepiot, who surrendered 17 homers (among 26 total) at what was the majors' seventh most-favorable home run environment in 2025. He's a capable, now built-up starting pitcher who could be ready to take another step forward into top-25 SP territory.

Heading into the 2025 season, Semien had been a model of reliability playing in the fifth-most games since he came into the league in 2015 while playing in three organizations with solid-to-spectacular production from his middle-infield positions. However, age appeared to catch up with him in 2025 as he had the worst season of his career at the plate which was eventually ended by a foot injury resulting from a foul ball. The Rangers, reticent to spend on the free-agent market, decided to trade Semien to the Mets for Brandon Nimmo, which could be a boon for a fully healthy Semien. He should now find himself nestled between Francisco Lindor and Juan Soto at the top of the Mets lineup providing him both ample RBI chances as well as plenty of run-scoring opportunities. He deserves one more chance from fantasy managers.

Bibee fell ill with food poisoning and missed his Opening Day assignment, which set the tone for a queasy start to the 2025 season. He posted a 5.85 ERA through his first four outings for the Guardians, but the right-hander settled in and ultimately peaked at the right time with a 0.86 ERA and 0.71 WHIP over his final 21 regular-season innings to help Cleveland overtake Detroit for the AL Central crown. While Bibee does not possess an overpowering fastball, he has five secondary pitches, including a changeup that helps him neutralize lefty batters. His strikeout rate fell precipitously last season and lagged well behind the top-end arms in MLB. His home-run rate is also trending in the wrong direction, but Bibee limits walks and has pitched especially well at home at Progressive Field in his three seasons in the big-league rotation.

An adjustment to his batting stance fueled a semi-breakthrough for Barger, who hit .291/.342/.568 with 14 home runs across a 60-game stretch early in the year and reflected significant boosts in Barrel and hard-hit metrics for the full season. He'd cool off later in the year, batting .205/.270/.360 with six homers over his final 49 regular-season games, before putting forth strong showings in the ALCS and World Series. Barger's skill set is not without its limitations, as he's a weak defender and struggles against lefties, making him both a platoon and late-inning removal risk. Still, he's capable enough in the power departments to warrant a late-round pick in larger mixed fantasy leagues.

Wells had a productive sophomore campaign for the Yankees despite some concerning trends in some of his performance indicators. Wells increased his aggressiveness at the plate, reducing his walk rate by nearly five full percentage points while his strikeout rate increased by over five percentage points. That resulted in his batting average falling further below the league average but still closer to an acceptable level for the catcher position. Wells still finished tied for fifth with 21 homers as a catcher and seventh with 71 RBI. Wells significantly improved his production against lefties, hitting six home runs while also batting .240 against southpaws. He also hit more homers on the road than at home, which goes against prevailing knowledge. His elite framing skills, as well as Ben Rice shifting to first base in 2026, should allow Wells to push for a career high in plate appearances this season.

Stanton didn't debut for the Yankees in 2025 until mid-June due to tendinitis in both elbows, but his presence was worth the wait as he posted 24 home runs and a .944 OPS, which was his best mark since his MVP campaign in 2017. He played in just 77 games but still provided plenty of run production with 66 RBI, though his actual runs total (36) was unsurprisingly much lower given his awful sprint speed. A 34.3 percent strikeout rate was the highest of Stanton's career, but he continues to hit the ball as hard as anyone in baseball. Expecting a repeat of that production over a larger sample wouldn't be wise, but Stanton has clubbed 24-plus homers each of the past five seasons and seems likely to do so again in 2026, even as he enters his age-36 season.

Dominguez has settled in as a whiff-generating, righty-dominating, short reliever -- and one who has been popular on the midseason trade market -- making him a good pickup for the bullpen-starved White Sox. His experience could prove useful in a prospective spring closer competition with Grant Taylor and Jordan Leasure, though Dominguez would still be helpful in holds leagues if the team prefers to go with a younger option.

Just 23 years old, Skenes is already authoring one heck of a career story. The No. 1 pick in the 2023 Draft, Skenes breezed to the majors after only 12 minor league starts and struck out 11 batters over six no-hit innings in his second career game on his way to winning the 2024 NL Rookie of the Year Award. He also became the first player in history to start the All-Star Game in both of his first two seasons, won the 2025 NL Cy Young Award and posted the lowest ERA (1.99) of any pitcher through his first 46 career starts. If there's a nit to pick, it's that his Pirates provided him such little run support (3.38 runs, third worst among ERA qualifiers) that he won only 10 games despite leading the majors in ERA in 2025. But hey, they're at least a little better offensively entering 2026? Skenes is as good a bet as any to lead all pitchers in fantasy points as well as the Player Rater.

Fresh off a breakthrough 2024 that saw him finish fourth in AL MVP voting, Henderson suffered an intercostal strain five games into spring training that seemed to derail him for most of last year. While he returned to action eight days into the regular season, he never seemed to recapture his prior power stroke, posting a .748 OPS and seven home runs in his first 50 games and reflecting a 5% decrease in his fly-ball rate for the full year. Henderson did, however, maintain his former line-drive stroke as well as his elite speed, swiping a pro-best 30 bases. Perhaps the winter's rest will help him recapture his prior pop. He's a name to track during spring training, as he'll enter 2026 at 24 years old, with MVP-caliber upside if he has a strong showing.

When a 131 wRC+ is your lowest mark since 2019, the bar is clearly high. It is fair to attribute Harper's dip to first-half elbow and wrist issues, the latter requiring a three-plus-week IL stint. However, a look under the hood reveals a low BABIP on outfield line drives that masked Harper's otherwise strong performance. His barrel, hard-hit and strikeout rates were consistent with prior seasons, but unfavorable batted-ball outcomes drove the drop in production. The good news is that a low outfield line-drive BABIP is not a sign of skills deterioration, just poor luck. Still, Harper missed 30 games, continuing a five-year pattern of IL visits. He remains a five-category contributor when healthy, as shown by 12 stolen bases in 14 attempts last season, though durability remains a concern. Harper is no longer a fantasy building block, but his draft stock remains high, as fear of missing out is a strong bias.

A first-half flexor strain limited Gilbert to just 25 starts spanning 131 innings, breaking his streak of three straight seasons with at least 185 frames. The injury interrupted his best season ever, at least in terms of his ERA estimators. His actual ERA ran a little higher than expected despite Gilbert setting a new personal best with a 32.3 percent strikeout rate. Gilbert's 26.5 K-BB percentage was the third highest among all pitchers logging at least 130 innings. That jump came after he shelved his cutter in favor of more four-seamers, splitters and sliders, though the adjusted mix led to a modest uptick in walks. Even so, Gilbert enters the season as a key piece of one of the league's top rotations, pitching roughly half his games in the most favorable park for pitchers.

Duran saw a decline in most areas in 2025 after his first All-Star season the year prior, losing nearly 30 points in batting average along with five homers and 10 steals from his 2024 totals. The outfielder still compiled valuable numbers with 16 HR and 24 SB across 157 regular-season games with the Red Sox while once again leading the American League in triples with 13. He also reached 40 doubles for the second consecutive year, with only Bobby Witt having more two-baggers over the last two seasons. Duran can fly, and his ability to take the extra base boosts his slugging percentage. The right-field dimensions at Fenway Park help the lefty hitter as well, though there have been rumors that Duran could eventually be traded. Even with the drop in performance and lingering uncertainty surrounding his future in Boston, Duran will remain a coveted piece in fantasy.

Contreras' fantasy production took a downturn in 2025, but it wasn't without explanation, as it was revealed in May that he was playing through a finger fracture dating back to the prior season -- one he endured for the near-entirety of last year. Despite that, his bat warmed along with the summer months, as a .286/.359/.465, 11-HR performance across his final 69 games offers hope that a rebound might be coming, especially after a winter of rest. Now 28, Contreras offers levels of patience and pop that few catchers can, and his 379 combined plate appearances (19% of his total) at DH over the past three seasons give him a rare volume advantage at the position. Continue to regard him one of the premier backstops.

The only player in history with at least 20 home runs and 20 stolen bases in each of his first five full MLB seasons, Arozarena joins Jose Ramirez as the only players at any point of their career to do that in each of the past five years. That provides Arozarena a strong, top-50 overall base for rotisserie fantasy play, even with his speed metrics declining slightly and this being his age-31 season. He'd need to continue improving his selectivity at the plate, however, to warrant consideration that soon in points leagues, where he's more of a mid-round selection in ESPN formats.

Greene took his career to another level in 2025, setting career highs in all run production categories, but with a strikeout rate of 30.7 percent. The young outfielder was an everyday player for Detroit because he was so good despite the fact his output against lefties remains a problem. Ten of Greene's 60 homers over the past two seasons have come off lefties, while he has been limited to a .216 average against southpaws. Meanwhile, along with the 50 homers against righties, Greene has a .278/.349./532 slash line versus them. His below-league-average strikeout rate from 2024 rose last season, which ultimately holds back how hopeful anyone can realistically be about BA improvement. The strikeout rate is the same against both righties and lefties. He's a four-category producer at risk of dropping to three if he can't curb the growing swing-and-miss in his stroke.

Strider's recovery from an April 2024 UCL repair -- his second such major elbow surgery -- got off to a solid start, as he had two games with double-digit strikeouts and averaged 12.3 fantasy points across his first 12 starts. Diminished fastball velocity and a ballooning walk rate would undermine him thereafter, as he had a 5.46 ERA and averaged just 4.3 fantasy points over his final 11 turns. It's difficult to pinpoint the reasons behind Strider's late struggles, with the easiest explanation being the challenging road back from UCL surgery, but his inconsistency is a concern for fantasy managers. When healthy, he has elite stuff that can make him one of the best pitchers in the game, but the risk involved makes him more of a middle-of-your-staff type come 2026 drafts.

Glasnow was unable to repeat his overall performance from 2024 when he set a new career high with just 134 innings of work, but did at least post a career-best 3.19 ERA over the 18 starts he made. The ERA was surprising since his walk rate jumped from 6.7 percent to 11.7 percent last season, dropping his normally stellar K-BB to a career-low 17.2 percent. Glasnow was still impossible to hit as the league hit .175 against him last season, which is not surprising since only Freddy Peralta, Jacob deGrom and Max Scherzer have been tougher to hit amongst all starting pitchers in baseball since Glasnow joined the league in 2016. Glasnow has some of the nastiest stuff in baseball, but he also has one of the most fragile bodies as something always breaks down. Expect 120 innings of valuable contributions but not much more.

Imanaga is back with the Cubs for 2026 despite the team declining his three-year club option, since the club still tagged him with the qualifying offer, which ultimately led to the pitcher accepting it to re-prove his market viability next offseason. Imanaga had a hamstring injury in early May which kept him off the mound for six weeks. He made 20 starts before September and recorded eight wins with a 3.08 ERA, and 0.93 WHIP. However, his final five starts in September included a 6.51 ERA with velocity decline and 10 homers allowed in just 27.1 innings of work. Despite the decent overall numbers, his strikeout numbers dropped significantly to 7.3 K/9. The motivation is there for a great 2026, but are the skills?

After hitting 232 home runs across a seven-year span (2018-24) in Japan, Okamoto suffered an elbow injury in a collision at first base, limiting him to a career-low 77 games. Ah, but what productive games they were! He hit .322/.411/.581 and made contact 87% of the time -- all of those career-best rates -- which bodes well for a smooth transition to the U.S. game. Okamoto figures to slide in at third base for the Blue Jays, where he'll benefit from hitting in the middle-to-lower portion of their deep lineup. As is the case with any Japanese hitter, his range of outcomes is wide due to the adjustment period required, but he's a well-rounded hitter who brings a lot of fantasy upside in the late rounds.

A submarining, ground ball-generating, righty-dominating short reliever, Rogers is one of the very best at his craft. However, you need to recognize the craft -- that of a locked-in, primary setup man rather than a flamethrower -- for what it is. He's a holds machine, owning 18% of the total number of 30-hold seasons across the past five seasons (he has four), with some of the most projectable ratios around. That's a nice thing to have in formats that reward setup men.

Winn's 2025 was going quite well until some knee discomfort in June revealed a slight tear in his meniscus which first required an injection and eventually led to him shutting his season down in mid-September to get a head start on the planned arthroscopic surgery. Winn had six homers heading into June but hit just three more the rest of the season, yet he was still able to steal seven bases in eight attempts on the bum knee. The injury helps explain away a lot of the traditional statistical decline Winn experienced in 2025 and gives reason to think he could be in store for improvement in 2026 assuming better luck on the health front. He may not get to 20 homers, but 20 steals with his speed and some increased opportunities on base is certainly possible. This is an underrated four-category contributor whose down 2025 offers a 2026 discount.

Volpe played through a partially torn labrum in his left shoulder for much of 2025 and underwent surgery in October, which is expected to sideline him for the start of 2026. The young shortstop provided fantasy managers with solid counting stats (19 home runs, 18 steals, 72 RBI and 65 runs in 153 games), but his .212/.272/.391 slash line left a lot to be desired. Playing through the injury obviously affected Volpe's offensive performance, but it's unclear exactly how much it influenced the actual results given that his .663 OPS was nearly identical to his first two big-league campaigns. He still has 20-20 upside and appears locked in as the Yankees' primary shortstop for another year, but a delayed start to 2026 and inconsistency make Volpe a volatile fantasy target.

Durbin gave Milwaukee and its fans an exciting immediate return on investment from trading Devin Williams in the offseason. Durbin leveraged a successful showing in the Arizona Fall League to earn a mid-April promotion to Milwaukee and never looked back. Durbin had the fifth-lowest strikeout rate for all batters with at least 500 plate appearances in 2025 and was a pest at the bottom of the Milwaukee lineup as a tough out at the plate while also being tough on the bases, stealing 18 bases in 24 attempts. Durbin will be hard pressed to hit more homers in 2026, but there is certainly room for batting average growth with better batted-ball fortunes and stolen bases with the accompanying improvement to his on-base percentage. The skills are there for a .280 average and 30-plus steals with better luck. Following his trade to the Red Sox, he'll likely start at third base.

There are five-tool talents, and then there's Witt. He was one of just two players to register at least 90th percentile Statcast metrics in terms of expected weighted on-base average (xwOBA), sprint speed and outs above average defensively (Corbin Carroll was the other) -- and Witt was the only one to also register at least a 90th percentile expected batting average. It's a skill set that solidifies his universal first-round fantasy status, and he'll enter 2026 at a prime-age 25. That his Royals moved the fences in at Kauffman Stadium this season can only help Witt's power prospects, as a return to the 30/30 form he displayed in 2023 and 2024 could be coming.

After a rocky first year in the U.S., year number two for Yamamoto was consistently excellent from start to finish -- literally. He won both the season's first game (in Japan in March) and its last, Game 7 of the World Series. In sum, he posted top-6 numbers across the league in ERA, WHIP and strikeout rate. Yamamoto's innings spike, totaling 211 frames between the regular season and postseason after 112 2/3 the year before, represents a slight concern following the rotator cuff issues he experienced in 2023, but his Dodgers are as careful with managing pitchers as any team in baseball. He's a fantasy ace and should be drafted in the opening rounds as such.

Raleigh's historic year -- he set single-season records for most home runs by a catcher (60) and drove in more runs (125) than any backstop had in 51 years -- is less subject to regression than you might think. He adopted an extremely fly ball-oriented approach at the plate, posting the highest qualified fly-ball rate in 13 years and the majors' fourth-best Barrel rate. Raleigh's raw power is as legitimate as anyone's in the game, even if it comes at the expense of many strikeouts and a low batting average. It makes him the top catcher, though his fantasy worth ultimately comes down to your league settings. In ESPN leagues, he's such a stalwart at a thin position that he's a borderline first-rounder. In deeper two-catcher leagues, Raleigh's 2025 headlines could cause him to be drafted too aggressively, ignoring the fact that 60 homers is a near impossibility to repeat.

A quadriceps injury he suffered in May derailed what was, at the time, a borderline MVP-caliber start to Bregman's Red Sox career. On May 14, for example, he was sixth among hitters in fantasy points, with significantly better contact-quality metrics than he had displayed in any prior year. Bregman never really recovered at the plate following his mid-July return, though his 154-game average over the three previous seasons (2022-24) suggests his finish was more aberration than the norm. The Cubs seemed to agree by granting him a five-year, $175 million guarantee, where they'll slot him high in what's a solid lineup. It's a good fit for Bregman, who is a great, building-block type of pick in points leagues thanks to his plate discipline and penchant for extra-base hits.

In his seventh season in the majors, Luzardo finally parlayed his high-90s fastball and whiff-generating sweeper and changeup into the breakthrough year fantasy managers had long anticipated. In fact, if not for back-to-back starts early in the season in which he surrendered a combined 20 earned runs, he might have garnered Cy Young votes and been a more prominent name heading into 2026 drafts. No matter, as that might make Luzardo a potential fantasy ace at the price of a mid-staff starter. He's no longer quite the injury risk he once was, with a pair of 32-start seasons in the past three years and, while he calls one of the more hitter-friendly environments his home, he gets some of the best lineup and bullpen support of any pitcher in the league.

Springer found the Fountain of Youth in 2025 with a .309 average, 32 homers and 18 steals across 140 regular-season games. He also tied for ninth in MLB in runs scored with 106 while often setting the table for a potent Blue Jays lineup. The incredible resurgence continued into October, with Springer posting an .899 OPS and four more homers during Toronto's run to the pennant. At 35 years old, Springer spent the majority of his time at designated hitter, though he still qualifies in the outfield. Prior to last season, Springer was in steady decline, bottoming out in 2024. However, in 2025 he looked nothing at all like a player on his last gasp in the major leagues. The DH tag should in theory help preserve his health in his late-30s.

Hoerner is that rare type of player who always seems to surprise fantasy managers with his year-end grades. He's a noted points-league standout, thanks to his elite contact skills -- he's one of just three players with at least an 85% qualified contact rate in all of the last three seasons. He also has a penchant for doubles and frequent appearances in the upper third of the Cubs lineup. However, Hoerner is also a successful rotisserie player, in that hitters capable of a .300 batting average and 30 stolen bases are a rarity nowadays -- there have only been six such seasons over the past four years, whereas there were six of them alone as recently as 2006. He should be regarded as a near-foundational piece in points leagues, in part due to how thin second base is. Just understand that if you take him early in a rotisserie league, you'll need to make up for his power shortcomings elsewhere on your roster.

After eight mediocre seasons between Philadelphia and Boston, Pivetta broke out in his first year with San Diego in 2025, going 13-5 with a 2.87 ERA and 0.99 WHIP across a career-high 181.2 innings during the regular season. Not only had Pivetta never posted an ERA under 3.00 prior to last year, he hadn't posted a mark under 4.00. A flyball pitcher, Pivetta has often struggled with homers, but he cut his home-run rate way down and was especially stingy with the long ball at home in Petco Park. Although he hadn't enjoyed a high level of success prior to 2025, Pivetta often tantalized with his strikeout rates. The late bloomer will continue to take the ball every fifth day for the Padres, and expectations should be heightened but realistic.

Perez once again fended off Father Time as he continues to outproduce catchers more than 10 years his junior. Ignore his lowest batting average since 2018; his xBA was his best since 2020, and his xSLG was tops since 2021. His strikeout, barrel and hard-hit rates were all better than in recent seasons. His bat speed dropped a tick, but after all, it was his 14th season, much of that time spent squatting his burly 6-foot-3 frame behind home plate. The Royals are doing a good job keeping the veteran fresh by frequently rotating him through first base and designated hitter. The catcher position continues to be replenished with promising young talent, but last season's perceived slide and another year of mileage could depress the price enough to make betting on Perez remaining a top-10 backstop worthwhile.

Gray and Lady Luck have been at odds for the last two years. In 2024, his ERA was pegged about a run too high by xFIP, and last season, his 4.28 ERA was deemed roughly a run higher than its estimators. His BABIP and HR/FB rate were elevated, while his LOB percentage was suppressed. Gray eclipsed 180 frames for the second straight season, which he had last accomplished in 2015. For the second consecutive season, his velocity slipped, but he waived his no-trade clause to join the Red Sox, who specialize in teaching pitchers to work off breaking balls and offspeed stuff, and Gray can throw multiple types. Gray's home runs have crept up over the past two seasons, and the Green Monster has a habit of turning routine flyballs into doubles, so Gray may need to get back in favor with Lady Luck. Father Time looms, but for now, Gray remains dependable.

Traded from Anaheim in November, Ward will be part of the new-look Orioles under new skipper Craig Albernaz in 2026. Ward's tenure with the Angels culminated in career highs in home runs (36) and RBI (103) last season, with the outfielder ranking in the top six in the AL in both categories, after previously topping out at 25 homers and 75 RBI in 2024. The right-handed slugger continues to mash lefties, and he at least hits for power against same-side arms if not for batting average. Ward added to his walk rate last season and his offensive contributions more than made up for his defensive limitations. Now 32, Ward should be in position to knock in the runners Pete Alonso leaves on base while batting in the middle of the everyday lineup in Baltimore.

Happ is entering the final year of his most recent contract, which is something to keep in mind for those who like factors such as contract years when targeting players. Happ has been a consistent on-base machine in recent seasons, but his batting average is now league average as the rest of the league has come down to his level. The switch hitter is at his best when facing righties as most of his homers come from the left side, but he has held his own hitting from the right side of the plate as well in recent years. His on-base abilities lock him in somewhere near the top of the Chicago lineup for 2026, but it will be a different batting order without the presence of Kyle Tucker, and the club's apparent reticence to spend big to replace him. Happ has been a 20/80/80/.240 producer for three straight years and expect a fourth.

After years of outperforming his expected ERA, Gallen didn't get much favor from Lady Luck in 2025. He had the eighth-widest ERA-xERA differential among qualifiers, he posted a career-worst 21.5% strikeout rate and he had an ERA over 4.00 in five out of six months. Still, Gallen continued to pitch effectively enough deep into games, his 33 starts being second-most and 192 innings eighth-most in the league. Plus, he had a 3.32 ERA over his final 11 starts. Back with the Diamondbacks after a long winter on the free-agent market, Gallen is a strong points-league option as one of the more durable starters out there.

A throwback type thanks to his elite-contact, batting average-but-minimal-pop hitting style, Arraez was a relative disappointment in 2025. He fell 12 points short of what would’ve been a fourth consecutive National League batting title, and the Padres struggled to find defensive positions at which to slot him due to his deficiencies in that regard. Teams might’ve seen similar issues with Arraez when considering him as a free-agent target, though the Giants ultimately saw enough in him to make him their everyday second baseman and probable No. 2 hitter. He’ll remain an underrated points league pick in that role, perhaps even from within the top 100 tier, while stabilizing roto teams’ batting averages.

Clement ended up being a key contributor for the Blue Jays throughout 2025, batting .277 with 35 doubles, 50 RBI and 83 runs in 157 games. He hit just nine home runs and stole six bags, both of which were drops from 2024 when he recorded 12 apiece. He makes a ton of contact and had low strikeout and walk rates (10.4 percent and 4.7 percent, respectively). Clement played in at least 29 games at third base, second base and shortstop while also making 15 appearances at first, which is more playing time than a utility player usually gets. Clement doesn't really profile as a true lineup regular, and he could be pushed out of a starting role, depending who else the Blue Jays sign this winter. He can have some deep-league appeal due to the high average, run potential and defensive versatility but likely won't get enough volume to be a reliable fantasy contributor.

The AL’s leading base stealer in both of the last two seasons, Caballero has the look of a single-category, roto-angled standout -- until you look closer. He improved his plate approach and the resulting walk rate (12.7%) last year, demonstrated above-average defense at five different positions (while also appearing in a sixth, in center field) and gave the Yankees reasonable cause to let him push Anthony Volpe for their starting shortstop job this spring. Caballero’s skill set indeed is better suited for roto play, where he’s a strong mid-round pick for his steals, but a standout March could make him a potential breakout candidate.

After four straight seasons of above-average production, Reynolds slipped to slightly below the norm, driven by a spike in his strikeout rate and a BABIP that didn't align with his batted-ball mix. He failed to gain the typical batting average boost that comes with more groundballs and line drives. His batting average dropped 30 points from the prior season, while his slugging finished 45 points below 2024. That said, his xBA was actually one point higher, and his xSLG was only 25 points short of the previous year. The downturn extended to the running game, as Reynolds went just 3-for-5 in steal attempts after going a combined 22-for-25 over the prior two seasons. Just 31 years old, Reynolds appears capable of a rebound if his strikeout and flyball rates move back toward earlier levels.

Grisham had an improbable 2025 season which saw him double his previous career high of 17 home runs, hitting 34 for the Yankees in his final year before free agency. He was one of the early advocates for the torpedo bat style, but that alone did not fuel this breakout power season as much as Grisham's overall deliberate approach to hitting. He is very patient at the plate and went hunting for fastballs early in counts, and often found them with 21 of his 34 homers coming from fastballs. Before you give Yankee Stadium's short porch too much credit, understand Grisham's home OPS was 200 points lower than it was on the road and he hit just 13 of his 34 home runs at Yankee Stadium last season. Grisham took the qualifying offer to firm up his free agency vitae with the thought Yankee Stadium cannot possibly punish him two consecutive seasons.

Baseball's greatest historical two-way player could be primed for his best season yet. On offense in 2025, Ohtani exceeded 50 home runs for a second consecutive season and stole 20-plus bases for a third straight year. On the mound, the Dodgers were uber-conservative with his recovery from his September 2023 elbow reconstruction, but Ohtani delivered per-start numbers in line with his pre-injury rates. His pitching usage also ramped up right in time for the playoffs, during which he became the first player in history to hit three home runs while also striking out 10 batters in one game in the Dodgers' NLCS clincher, triggering memories of his 2022, when he scored 411 fantasy points as a hitter and 475 as a pitcher. As the Dodgers surely will, so must you manage his daily utility -- he can be used as a DH or pitcher, but not both --  but Ohtani's potential puts him head and shoulders ahead of the pack.

Much of the storyline surrounding Sanchez during last year's breakthrough was his second straight year of increased sinker velocity -- he went from 92.1 mph in 2023 to 94.5 in 2024 to 95.4 in 2025 -- but the real story was the advances he made with his changeup. He struck out 130 batters with that pitch alone, the most by any pitcher in six years. Sanchez dodged a minor scare with his elbow in April, swiftly rebounding to post more quality starts than any pitcher, as well as the third-best ERA from that point forward. His combination of pinpoint control, extreme ground ball repertoire and top-shelf stuff make him one of the safest investments on the pitching side (if there is such a thing in this modern age). Draft Sanchez as your fantasy ace with confidence.

After finishing seventh among pitchers in fantasy points over the final four months of 2024, Brown followed things up with six straight months of near-identical production (he'd finish sixth this time). A modest boost to his swinging-strike rate, while maintaining his elevated average fastball velocity, fueled a consistently excellent year, during which he never went more than three outings between quality starts. Brown appears to have leveled off, but he has done so as one of the premier talents at his position. He should be one of the first starting pitchers off your draft board in any format.

Fresh off a career year in 2024 and with his team moving to one of baseball's most hitter-friendly environments in Sacramento last season, Rooker seemed primed to potentially take another step forward. Come year's end, his 2025 had an eerie 2023 look to it, albeit with some key improvements. He traded some of his power for contact, with his fly-ball rate plummeting by 4% but his contact rate improving by roughly the same margin. The end result probably prevents Rooker from winning future home run crowns, but for as long as he calls Sutter Health Park his home, he'll be good for at least his 2025 numbers, if not better.

A rotator cuff strain cost Ragans three months of 2025, entirely thwarting his rise to becoming one of fantasy baseball's premier starters. That, coupled with a groin strain that cost him 19 days in May/June, cast him as somewhat of an injury risk entering 2026, but be aware that these ailments did little to diminish his excellent skill set. Ragans' final two regular-season starts (among the three he made in September) had him striking out 18 out of 35 batters, with similar levels of velocity and swing-and-miss rates to those pre-injury. He'll need careful examination during spring training for any lingering health issues, but a dominant Ragans in March could help make a case for him to be a top-10 fantasy starter come draft day.

For the first time since 2017, Buxton played more than two-thirds of his team's games last season, though he still made two more trips to the IL (totaling 29 days). OK, we'll still call it a win! Better health led to a complete restoration of his top-shelf raw power and speed metrics and, thanks in part to a career high in plate appearances, he managed another personal best with 35 home runs and was a perfect 24-for-24 stealing bases. Consider it a reminder of what Buxton can contribute at his best, as he's still a close-to-prime 32 years of age albeit with sterling speed metrics. His extensive injury history will -- and should --always keep your draft-day expectations in check. He's also still preferable in rotisserie than in points leagues, but his upside when healthy warrants mid-round consideration.

Bellinger's skill set is a cavalcade of underlying metric-busting magic. Here are his percentile rankings in various Statcast metrics over the past three seasons combined: 21st in bat speed, 25th in hard-hit rate and 39th in Barrel rate. Nevertheless, Bellinger's three-year averages during that same time are a .281 batting average, 24 homes, 91 RBI and 14 steals -- and he has even earned MVP votes in two of those seasons! Having as elite a contact rate as he does certainly helps, as does his extreme fly ball leaning (which makes him a particularly good fit for Yankee Stadium). Bellinger isn't the MVP example he was in 2019, but he's a plenty useful fantasy player all around, and a near-star in points leagues.

Last season was a career year for Langeliers, and there were two specific things which held him back from getting even more attention: an oblique injury which cost him some time in the summer, and Cal Raleigh stealing all the spotlight. Langeliers was on a 40-homer pace, and while many will credit the comforts of Sutter Health Park in Sacramento, that would be a mistake as Langeliers hit 19 of his 31 home runs on the road. He increased his power output while also cutting down his strikeout rate from the previous season. The club went as far as to use Brent Rooker in the field despite his defensive limitations to allow Langeliers some half-days off at DH. Langeliers' draft stock has improved as much as any player in baseball, and with all arrows pointing in the right direction, he should be one of the top fantasy catchers in MLB in 2026.

Adames entered his first season with the Giants facing two uncertainties: how the move to Oracle Park would affect his bat, and whether his running game would hold up. The shift from hitter-friendly American Family Field to a park that suppresses offense showed up in his surface numbers, but not in his skills. His 108 wRC+ matched his final three years in Milwaukee, indicating his performance held steady after park adjustment, even if his 2025 wOBA dipped. His barrel and hard-hit rates ticked up slightly, while his strikeout rate reached a three-year high, keeping his batting average volatile despite power that plays anywhere. He attempted fewer steals, largely reflecting team philosophy. Overall, Adames continues to profile as a mid-tier shortstop.

Estevez is coming off a fantastic season for Kansas City which saw him lead all of baseball with 42 saves for an 82-win club. Any concerns the talented Lucas Erceg would steal saves were quickly set aside as Estevez refused to give up any ground in the bullpen. He does not have the big strikeout rates of other closers in the game, but over the past two seasons, Estevez has the third-lowest ERA of all active closers and does not get himself into trouble with walks or homers. The fact Kansas City plays in a high rate of late and close games due to an inconsistent offense only helps Estevez get the ball on a regular basis. Estevez is not the sexiest closer, but he gets the job done and he should one again save 30-plus contests in 2026.

Reliever ERAs can be deceptive, and Hoffman was a clear example of that for several years. He beat his estimators in four straight seasons, running an ERA well below what his peripherals suggested. It led to expectations of regression, and his 4.37 ERA last year was his highest since 2021. Even so, a 3.21 SIERA suggests the results were inflated. While there was some skills slippage, potentially tied to a move into the AL East, the biggest problem was a sharp spike in home runs, as his 1.99 HR/9 ranked among the league's worst. Hoffman still recorded a career-high 33 saves, fourth most in baseball, but frequent long balls are a quick way to lose managerial trust, particularly in high-leverage spots like the postseason. He remains part of Toronto's saves picture, but opportunities will have to be earned, and limiting home runs will be critical.

The active career leader in saves (476), Jansen's skills gradually eroded as he progressed through his mid-30s, but the Tigers see enough potential in him at age 38 that they signed him as their presumptive closer. He has saved at least 25 games in each of the past 13 uninterrupted MLB seasons, but 2025 saw him register career worsts in strikeout rate (24.4%), Statcast expected ERA (3.74) and hard-hit rate allowed (44.6%). Jansen is a role-driven, middle-of-your-staff type for fantasy purposes, the promise of save chances in Detroit buoying his value -- so long as he pitches effectively enough to keep the job.

Lodolo made huge strides in 2025, posting a 4.8% walk rate that ranked sixth among pitchers with at least 20 starts, while generating many swings-and-misses on pitches out of the zone -- he had the fourth-best chase rate among that same group -- before injuries largely interrupted his final two months. At the time, he had scored the 20th-most fantasy points among pitchers. Whether those injuries (a blister, an illness, a right groin issue) represent a recurring pattern is in question, but Lodolo could be on the verge of a full-season breakthrough with the adjustments he has made. He's a pitcher to watch during spring training, as he'd have a top-25 starter's ceiling with a standout March.

Diaz's wRC+ declined for the second straight season despite a gain in power. Over the prior two years, his batting average closely tracked his xBA, but last season he finished 16 points below expected, driven largely by an unusually low line-drive BABIP. He also posted a career-low hard-hit rate, working against batting average. Added loft did push his barrel rate to a career high, and he paired that with the lowest strikeout rate of his career. Diaz grades as a below-average defender, so reversing the offensive slide will be important if he is to remain among the most heavily used backstops after his 567 plate appearances ranked sixth among catcher-eligible players last season. More line drives falling in would help, but he also needs to hit the ball with more authority and with greater selectivity.

Murakami, who hit 223 home runs over a six-year span (2019-24) in Japan, put off a move to the States one winter ago, only to suffer an injury-plagued 2025 campaign. Between elbow surgery and a nagging oblique issue, he played only 69 games, though his power potential upon his return was as excellent as ever. He hit 24 homers, slugged .659 and had .373 isolated power for the season. The White Sox took a $34 million chance on him to play first base, which at least offers additional positional flexibility for his fantasy managers. Just 26 years old, Murakami is a �three true outcomes� style lefty slugger, which could elicit within White Sox fans memories of Adam Dunn (the Chicago version) on the high end, or Daniel Palka on the low end. Fantasy managers would be best to split the difference and draft accordingly.

Stott put together a respectable if unspectacular campaign as the Phillies' regular second baseman in 2025, hitting 13 home runs and stealing 24 bags across 147 regular-season games. He sat occasionally against left-handed pitching and did little against southpaws when given the opportunity with a .575 OPS and one homer in 123 PA without the platoon edge. A plus on defense, Stott figures to remain Trea Turner's double-play partner in Philadelphia for the foreseeable future despite his shortcomings. Citizens Bank Park is hitter friendly and Stott isn't asked to carry much of the load offensively, for better or worse. Manager Rob Thomson experimented with Stott in the leadoff spot last season but eventually settled on him being a lower-third bat even against right-handed pitching.

Aranda's counting stats from 2025 don't really stand out on the surface as he finished with 14 homers, 59 RBI and 56 runs, but he remarkably did most of that damage before the end of July when a collision with Giancarlo Stanton sidelined him for nearly two full months. Overall for the year, he delivered a .316/.393/.489 slash line in 106 games, priming him for a full breakout if he can stay healthy in 2026. Aranda's batted-ball metrics ranked among the best in the league, so there shouldn't be much worry about that elite performance being luck driven. He also returned for three games at the end of the regular season and went 4-for-12 with two long balls, eliminating concern about injury carryover. Aranda should bat in the heart of Tampa Bay's batting order in 2026, and fantasy managers are likely going to have to invest heavily to nab him on draft day.

Fantasy managers love Castro’s positional flexibility, and now they’ll love another thing about him: He’ll call Coors Field his home. Besides his defensive utility, Castro’s most marketable skill is his speed, but he’s capable enough with the bat to capitalize upon the favorable hitting environment. He’s an ideal round-out-your-roster type, able to be mixed and matched for his Coors games and against weaker starting pitchers. Just don’t expect any miracles when he’s playing on the road.

Westburg's output closely matched the prior season, though injuries again played a central role. A broken hand limited him to 107 games in 2024 and wiped out much of the second half, while last year brought a late-April hamstring injury sidelining him for almost six weeks, followed by a mid-August ankle sprain that cost him another month. The skill gains he showed before the 2024 injury didn't carry over, and his plate discipline has slipped from his minor-league days, with a walk rate just under five percent across the past two seasons. Improved health and greater patience could allow more of his power to surface. He isn't an aggressive base stealer by nature, and the injuries further reduced his running. Limited to 85 games, Westburg also came up three games shy of second-base eligibility in most formats.

Paredes' 2025 season can best be summed up by what could have been. The third baseman hit 20 homers in 102 games while being forced to miss two full months with an acute hamstring tear that initially looked like a season-ending injury. Paredes' extreme pull and flyball approach are an ideal fit for his home stadium, yet just 11 of his 20 home runs came at Daikin Park. Paredes previously hit 31 homers around the challenges of Tropicana Field and the changing of the dimensions in Baltimore in 2023, so we know what a full season of his approach is capable of, but that same approach also leaves him quite susceptible to batting average risk, because his batted balls that do not leave the yard are either cans of corn or routine groundball outs to the left side due to his slow foot speed. He might hit 40 home runs in 2026, but he may also struggle to hit .240.

Manzardo exhausted his rookie eligibility with 156 plate appearances in 2024, but he got in his first full MLB campaign last season and produced 27 home runs, 70 RBI, 47 runs and a .234/.313/.455 slash line in 142 games. He did most of his damage against right-handed pitching with a .789 OPS, though he still slugged .419 versus lefties. Manzardo doesn't offer much defensively but still made 56 appearances at first base, so he'll have eligibility there rather than solely as a designated hitter. He should be a steady presence in Cleveland's lineup in 2026 but may not have true everyday volume given his struggles against southpaws, though his power potential could help him see more chances than a standard platoon player.

Fantasy managers have been (im)patiently awaiting the return of Guerrero's 2021 AL MVP runner-up form. When he finally displayed it, it was during a time when few could reap the rewards. We're talking the 2025 playoffs, where he hit .397/.494/.795 with eight homers in 18 games. That's not to substantially knock Guerrero for his regular-season exploits, as the past five seasons have seen him post the fifth-most fantasy-point average (478.6), the second-most total hits (893) and third-most total bases (1,546). He's a model of consistency with a star's ability to shine at any moment, even if those are sometimes seemingly selective. Still a prime-age 27, Guerrero should be one of your first couple of picks, even if he's not necessarily worthy of being the first.

Don't let the persistent trade rumors swirling around him dissuade you that Skubal is as good a choice to lead your fantasy pitching staff as anyone. He's coming off back-to-back Cy Youngs, and has made consistent, notable improvements in almost every statistical category across his six MLB seasons. Skubal set personal bests in ERA, WHIP, walk rate, K/BB rate, whiff rate and rate of hard contact allowed in 2025. Since July 1, 2023, he has a 2.37 ERA and MLB-leading totals in both wins (38) and strikeouts (571). He's also entering his contract year -- the very reason for said trade rumors -- which, while hardly a guarantee as a motivating factor, assures he'll play 2026 at full bore, and with a team that will provide him the necessary support to again thrive.

Wood got off to a torrid start to his first full MLB season, batting .278/.381/.534 with 24 homers in 95 first-half games to earn himself an All-Star appearance. The holes in his ground ball-oriented swing, however, caught up with him thereafter, and he hit just .223/.301/.388 with an MLB-leading 105 strikeouts the rest of the way. Wood will need to address those shortcomings, or add some loft to his swing, in order to develop into a true offensive superstar, but few players have the kind of top-shelf metrics in terms of bat speed and contact quality. He's a player to watch during March to see what kinds of adjustments he makes, though as is he's a high-ceiling, early-to-mid-round selection with more upside in rotisserie than points leagues.

Through four months of 2025, Crow-Armstrong seemed on track for top-level MVP votes, in rotisserie terms providing more earnings than any player other than Aaron Judge and Shohei Ohtani. Regression and his own free-swinging nature at the plate hit Crow-Armstrong hard over the final two months, however, as he hit just .188/.237/.295 and struck out in more than 25% of his trips to the plate. In his defense, Crow-Armstrong's elite speed gives him a steady valuation base in rotisserie leagues, and his Platinum Glove-caliber defense assures him of regular playing time -- which helps boost his points-league value. Improved patience would be his ticket to stardom in the latter, but in the former, he's already a building-block draft pick.

After a miserable, injury-marred 2024, Bichette rebounded last season with the same kind of elite-contact, line drive-oriented approach he exhibited during his 2021-23 peak -- only to see his regular season (and early postseason) interrupted by yet another injury, this time a knee sprain. It rekindled the durability question, which has sapped almost all of the above-average speed he once possessed. The Mets are banking on Bichette's per-game hitting numbers, which were excellent across five months, as being more representative of his skill set, and we tend to agree. Still, we'd understand if his injury risk causes you to balk at the cost of a top-50 overall pick.

Suarez's "HR or nothing" approach at the plate paid its biggest dividends in 2025, from his four-homer game in late April, to his season-ending career bests of 49 HR, 118 RBI, 40.9% fly ball and 47.6% hard-hit rates. Shifting his swing in that direction over the years has put him at an elevated risk of low batting averages, however, as well as peaks and valleys in his performance. That's not the kind of profile that seems likely to age well, and Suarez will play most of 2026 at 34 years of age. Expect some regression in the power department, though he should still put the ball over the fence frequently enough to remain a top-10 fantasy third baseman.

Widely regarded as the top prospect in all of baseball, Griffin's skill set is regarded so highly that he has generated some chatter that he could break camp with the Pirates and perhaps even win the NL  Rookie of the Year Award, despite only one year's pro experience under his belt. What a debut year it was, as he hit 21 homers, stole 65 bases, hit .333/.415/.527, played solid shortstop and performed equally well across three competitive levels through Double-A. Griffin is the kind of future-MVP-caliber prospect that dynasty league managers should build around. Redraft managers should scoop him up instantly upon his promotion. If you've got space to stash him, a realistic ETA in Pittsburgh might be before mid-season.

Coming off a 6.14 ERA and an unremarkable spring, Palencia opened the season at Triple-A Iowa before being recalled in mid-April to add bullpen depth. He quickly impressed, posting a 1.20 ERA and 0.80 WHIP with 15 strikeouts across 15 innings, which earned him a save opportunity amid struggles from Ryan Pressly and an injury to Porter Hodge. Though he blew his first chance, Palencia converted his next five save opportunities and retained the job until a shoulder injury sidelined him in early September. He returned for the final week in lower-leverage work. With the Cubs adding quality setup options, Palencia has a clear path to build on last year's team-leading 23 saves. While his track record is lacking, a repeat performance could elevate him into a higher tier.

Whether due to injuries or the aging process, Trout is no longer the perennial MVP candidate he once was. Though he played 130 games in 2025 -- more than he had in the previous two seasons combined or in any single year since 2019 -- he hit just .232 with his lowest OPS in any full year (.797). Trout no longer catches up with breaking stuff at his prior Hall of Fame levels, leading to high strikeout totals and lower batting averages, though his power remains excellent (.207 ISO and 93rd-percentile Statcast Barrel rate). The result is a player now similarly valued in roto and points leagues, one now best left to filling out your lineup rather than leading it.

The Dodgers repeated as champions, but Hernandez did not contribute to the same level during the 2025 regular season as the Regression Monster caught up to him. He spent time on the injured list in May with an adductor strain and also missed time after fouling a pitch off his foot. Ultimately, he lost eight homers, 10 RBI and seven steals from his 2024 totals, along with more than 100 points in OPS. The slugger was still a net positive but only slightly due to his deteriorating defense in right field. With Shohei Ohtani taking up the DH spot, Hernandez has to play the outfield to remain in the Los Angeles lineup. For now, he projects to remain a regular, but his poor defense at 33 years old leaves open some downside risk in regards to playing time.

Schlittler went from being a prospect afterthought entering the 2024 minor-league season to becoming the first pitcher in postseason history to pitch eight scoreless innings of at least 12 strikeouts (with zero walks) in the 2025 Wild Card Series. Such demonstrates the magnitude of his unexpected breakthrough. Thanks to his improved, 98.0-mph fastball and cutter, he scored the 19th-most fantasy points from the date of his July 9 debut forward, with stellar underlying metrics that support his ability to approach or match the effort over a full 2026. Schlittler is a strong mid-round, middle-of-your-staff pick for fantasy purposes, assuming the back issues that popped up as spring training dawned don't become a lingering issue.

The Cardinals' top prospect entering 2026, Wetherholt would make a lot of sense for them in their Opening Day lineup, considering their shift to a rebuild and February’s trade of Brendan Donovan. Wetherholt has torn through three minor-league levels in just 14 months (and 138 games), batting a robust .314/.416/.562 with 10 homers and nine steals in 47 season-concluding games for Triple-A Memphis last year. He has an elite plate approach, which should ease his transition to the majors and make him particularly attractive in points leagues. He's a dynasty building block and, if he breaks camp as the team's second baseman or shortstop as expected, would be a top Rookie of the Year candidate.

Smith was one of the stories of spring training last year when his long-shot bid to make Houston's Opening Day roster was successful, but the harsh realities of Major League Baseball eventually set in. The third-baseman-turned-outfielder hit the skids in the summer months and finished with a .154/.247/.242 line in the second half. GM Dana Brown acknowledged after the 2025 season that Smith could require more time back on the farm, pointing to the need for greater consistency. It wasn't all bad as Smith had his moments, including a two-homer game in April, but the way his rookie year ended suggests a reset may be necessary. The upside is still there long term for the 2024 first-round pick whom the Astros acquired from the Cubs as part of the return for Kyle Tucker.

Throughout 2025, Steer was held back by some upper-back issues which never put on him on the injured list but did hamper his ability to drive the ball with authority on a consistent basis. Steer once again hit 20-plus homers for a third consecutive season, and he was pacing to set a new career high if not limited by the nagging injury. He lost nearly 90 plate appearances from the previous two seasons both due to injury and the club giving Sal Stewart some extra time at first base down the stretch. It was surprising to see Steer's stolen-base production fall off as much as it did in 2025 with Terry Francona's lead foot taking over the running game, but that too could easily return if Steer is 100 percent healthy for 2026. The 2023 season was a great one for him with an .820 OPS, but Steer has yet to replicate that level of production.

Leiter's adjustment to big-league competition has been slow, but appreciate his 2025 growth for what it was. He posted a 3.28 ERA, seven quality starts and a 26.3% strikeout rate across 13 second-half starts and lowered his walk rate to 7.0% over his final nine outings. Equipped with a high-90s fastball and maturing slider and changeup, Leiter could be ready to take a big step forward in 2026. He has the top prospect pedigree, making him one of the more potentially profitable prospective late-round picks for your draft.

Nelson made some changes to his approach in 2025, and the results followed. He remains a fastball-heavy pitcher, but against lefties he used breaking balls rather than changeups as his secondary offerings and greatly improved his results. Lefties had hit .267/.328/.482 off him the previous two seasons, but the new approach led to a .191/.25/.309 outcome in 2025. Nelson also found more success pitching at home, which had been a tremendous problem for him each of the previous two seasons. Nelson did not even join the Arizona rotation on a full-time basis until early June but went 5-2 with a 3.38 ERA and 1.10 WHIP over those 20 starts. Nelson looks primed to repeat his 2025 success with more innings as a full-time starter who has worked hard to reduce some overall weak spots in his game.

Although his .224/.352/.393, 8-HR stat line through the first 55 games of 2025 gave the guise of a $765 million contract hangover, Soto's first season with the Mets, on the whole, was anything but. Over the next four months and change, he was fantasy baseball's highest-scoring player (411 points), finishing the year with a career-best 43 home runs while delivering his third consecutive season with at least 100 RBI, 125 walks and a .900 OPS. In an unusual twist, Soto also stole 38 bases, more than he had in the previous four years combined, as he went on an unreal run (pardon the pun) over the season's final two months, seemingly in a quest to join the 40/40 club.
