That is the facet of his game where regression seems likeliest to strike in 2026, but Soto, still a prime-age 27, remains one of the best players to build around in points leagues and a first-round pick in rotisserie formats.

Given a chance to play daily for the first time, Caminero broke through in a big way in 2025, his 45 home runs tied for the fourth most in history by a player 22 or younger. It wasn't entirely fueled by the team's one-year stint at hitter-friendly George M. Steinbrenner Field, either, as Caminero hit more homers on the road (23) than at home (22), though the venue indeed benefited him as a hitter, his OPS 211 points higher in his home games. The move back to pitchers' heaven Tropicana Field for 2026 will raise some alarm bells for Caminero's prospective fantasy managers, but he has some of the best bat speed in baseball and enough contact ability to maintain a high level of impact, regardless of venue. He also finished the year on a high note, batting .291/.353/.615 with 17 homers over his final 47 games, 30 of which were played on the road. Caminero is a franchise building block for fantasy purposes.

Chisholm and Yankee Stadium represented the perfect marriage, as his first full season in pinstripes saw him pull a career-high 53.3% of batted balls and hit 33.2% in the air (his second-highest single year rate), resulting in his first 30/30 campaign. It did, however, cost him in batting average, as his .242 was his full-season worst, putting more emphasis on his need to steal bases to make up the difference for fantasy. Chisholm's declining speed metrics, and the groin issue that made him more conservative on the basepaths around midseason, raise slight concerns, but he's still one of the better early-round picks you'll find for rotisserie formats. Improving patience over the past two seasons also helps his points-league value, where he's worth a look, albeit one or two rounds later.

The aging curve has clearly affected Betts, as his 2025 season saw him post personal worsts in almost every statistical category, not the least of which were his .732 OPS, 35.8% hard-hit rate and 4.3% attempted steals rate. In his defense, however, he dealt with a stomach illness at the season's onset -- something that caused him to lose close to 20 pounds and affected his mechanics at the plate. Betts is fortunately in one of the absolute best environments for propping up counting numbers, as he's surrounded by a cavalcade of lineup all-stars, and he's a contact hitter whose floor isn't as perilous as most. Set your expectations at his three-year averages of a .284 batting average, 26 home runs, 88 RBI and 13 steals and you should be happy with him for the asking price.

After months of rumors, Peralta was traded from the Brewers to the Mets in January as he enters his final season before free agency. The right-hander put together a career year in 2025, leading the National League in wins with 17 to go along with a career-low 2.70 ERA across 33 starts for Milwaukee. Peralta has now reached the vaunted 30-start and 200-strikeout thresholds each of the last three years, cementing his status as a legitimate frontline starter in MLB, with three excellent secondary pitches making up for a mediocre fastball. It's entirely possible that 2025 will end up being the zenith of his career, as everything went right for him during the regular season. Regression should be built into the draft price, but the skills and track record at 29 years old make Peralta worthy of a significant investment.

If you believe in such folly, it's an even-numbered year, so based upon past patterns, Cease is destined for greatness in 2026. He's a modern-day Bret Saberhagen, but with strikeouts! Cease's FIP tells a more rational tale, as he has fluctuated by less than two-thirds of a run in the category over the past five seasons, a signal that luck factors have been friendly to him in those even-numbered campaigns, but harsh in odd years. What fuels bounce-back chatter with Cease isn't the date on the calendar, but rather his new team's defense, as the Blue Jays are significantly better in the field than were the 2025 Padres. See, luck can be controlled � somewhat, at least. Don't let Cease slip beyond the first few rounds of your draft.

A 4-for-35 showing in the postseason couldn't spoil what was an overall offensive breakout for the Brewers' second baseman. Turang went from ranking third in MLB with 50 steals in 2024 to 28th with just 24 steals last season, but he added surprising power and piled up the runs and RBI for a Milwaukee team that ranked third in scoring, with fantasy managers happily accepting the tradeoff for more well-rounded production. Overall, Turang added more than 30 points in batting average and nearly 130 points in OPS to finish neck and neck with Jazz Chisholm at second base in rotisserie leagues. He hits left-handed pitching well enough and seems to have established a new performance baseline, though the batted-ball profile portends a BA closer to .260 than .280 in 2026 and beyond.

Busch is coming off a tremendous sophomore season which saw him flex his power to another level while improving his strikeout rate five full percentage points. Busch hit 30 of his 34 homers against righties and was quite neutralized by lefties all season, and he found road parks to be more conducive to his homers with 21 of the 34 coming away from Wrigley Field. Busch may also be one of the few players to hit 30 or more home runs in a season during which his most common position in the batting order was leadoff, as he led off for the Cubs in 52 contests last season. Should that usage continue, Busch is likely to score more runs than he drives in, but he did still manage 90 RBI last season. If he and Ian Happ flip in the projected lineup around Nico Hoerner, Busch could drive in 100-plus.

Sean Murphy's cracked rib in March paved the way for Baldwin to step in as the Braves' Opening Day catcher, and despite Murphy's lingering presence all year, the lefty slugger made enough of his opportunity that he ultimately captured NL Rookie of the Year honors. Baldwin's is a rare combination of contact, contact quality and raw power. He joined fellow catcher Alejandro Kirk as baseball's only players with at least 400 plate appearances, 10% Statcast Barrel, 45% hard-hit and 80% contact rates. Baldwin also excelled against same-handed pitchers, his almost complete skill set diminishing the chances of a sophomore slump. Although Murphy remains in Atlanta, Baldwin should handle the bulk of the catching duties -- perhaps in a straight platoon, but that's still plenty to make him one of the position's top picks.

The No. 2 overall pick in the 2024 Draft, Burns soared to the majors after only 13 minor-league starts, then used his 98.7-mph fastball and filthy slider to post four games of double-digit strikeouts in his first eight, as well as a 37.7% K rate over that time. While he had some issues with lefties and missed time due to a flexor strain, he did return to make five solid relief appearances and figures to make the Reds' rotation out of spring training. Burns has some work to do on improving a pitch to use against lefties, and he's a little too fly ball-oriented to avoid issues with homers in Great American Ball Park, but he's one of the most intriguing breakthrough candidates among pitchers. He's a dynasty league building block and a mid-round target in redraft formats.

Eovaldi threw a shutout in his second start of 2025 and pitched like a Cy Young candidate with a 1.73 ERA and 0.85 WHIP over 22 total starts for the Rangers before a rotator cuff strain ended his season in late August. The right-hander then underwent sports hernia surgery in October. While ostensibly healthy heading into 2026, Eovaldi should be considered a long shot to make 30 starts, something he's done only once over the last decade. Regression to his numbers seems inevitable, though tangible improvement can be found behind his success last season, as he dialed back his fastball usage in strategic fashion while trimming his walk rate back to elite territory. As he enters his age-36 season, the wheels are in danger of falling off, but Eovaldi is a legitimate ace when healthy.

Nimmo put together another productive campaign in 2025, slugging 25 homers with 92 RBI, both career highs, to go along with 81 runs and 13 steals across 155 games with the Mets. Last season marked his fourth straight reaching 150 games, as Nimmo continues to distance himself from the injury issues that plagued him earlier in his career. In November, he was traded to the Rangers amidst rumors of a rift with former teammate Francisco Lindor, a move that looks like a wash for Nimmo in many respects. The outfielder gave up a bit in terms of OBP and was more aggressive in recent years as he took on more of a run-producer role, but he has the plate skills to transition back to leadoff duty if Texas prefers to go that route.

For what seemed like the umpteenth year in a row, Snell was excellent when available to his fantasy managers � which didn't happen especially often. Among the 61 pitchers who have made at least 87 starts over the last four seasons, he ranks first in strikeout rate (31.9%), second in ERA (2.76), fifth in fantasy points per start (13.9) and seventh in hard-hit rate allowed (34.8%). The problem? That's exactly the number of starts Snell made in that time, which is under 22 per year. It's remarkable that he has been able to maintain such a high level of productivity around his many absences, but credit the Dodgers for being among the best at maximizing pitcher workloads and utility when available. We see no reason for that to change now. So, how lucky do you feel?

Now, where did that come from? Montgomery arrived in Chicago in early July and quickly went on an uncharacteristic power surge. Over a 37-game span a few weeks after his recall, he hit 18 home runs, matching his entire 2024 total across 130 minor-league games. And that's not to say that he can't do it again, as he had strong underlying hard-contact metrics, but his 17.2% HR/FB rate, which was eighth-highest in the league from his debut date forward, hints that there'll be some pullback. Montgomery might need to improve his plate approach in order to take another step forward in 2026. As it is, he's a late-round pick for mixed-league play.

The Astros thought they had solved their problems at first base when they signed Walker to a three-year, $60 million contract in December of 2024, but he mostly ended up just being the club's latest headache. The veteran first baseman struggled out of the gate with a .210/.273/.357 slash line through the first two months of the season, and he was never quite able to dig out of that hole. Walker showed signs of life in July and August with an .831 OPS, but that type of production was the expectation for the full season, not just two months. He still launched 27 home runs -- his fourth straight year with at least 26 -- and had respectable RBI (88) and run (72) totals, but the lack of consistency was a major issue. Walker is a decent candidate to bounce back in 2026, with his power and run production providing a solid floor despite the fact he's coming off a disappointing season.

The No. 2 overall pick in the 2023 Draft and a top-10 overall prospect entering his 2025 rookie season, Crews put forth solid power (7 HR) and speed (11 SB) numbers across his first 45 games, though his free-swinging nature (27.7 K%) led to a miserable, .196 batting average. An oblique strain would then cost him nearly three months, after which point he delivered more of the same, but with the same 50%-plus ground ball rate that must improve for him to truly realize his full power potential. Crews should get a long look for a starting role during spring training and, as he matures, he'll at least provide a solid stolen bases total for roto managers. He's more of a profitable late-rounder there than in points leagues, though he still has a high long-term ceiling for any fantasy format.

Coming off what was a top-10 fantasy starter's 2024, Miller's follow-up campaign was effectively ruined by bone spurs in his elbow, the ailment sending him to the IL twice and nearly doubling his ERA. Though his fastball velocity and whiff rate on his splitter improved over the season's final six weeks, his ERA over that time was nevertheless 5.62 and he couldn't find consistency at any point all year. Miller did avoid offseason surgery, but only spring training can demonstrate whether the winter's rest has helped him. He still has that ace-caliber stuff when healthy, so a strong spring would make him a potentially profitable late-round pick.

Caglianone had one of the more disappointing rookie seasons in 2025, posting the worst batting average (.157) and OPS (.532) among those with at least 200 plate appearances, while sporting one of the league's worst chase rates. But, to be fair, he was also only a little over a year removed from being a two-way player at Florida, with only 95 games of minor-league experience focusing on hitting alone at the time. Caglianone did flash gaudy bat speed and Barrel metrics, and the 20 homers he hit in 66 minor-league games underscore his massive potential in that department. The Royals' decision to shrink the outfield dimensions at Kauffman Stadium should also help him. If Caglianone is swinging well in Cactus League play, make sure to scoop him up late in the hopes he's ready to break through at age 23.

Musgrove missed all of last season while rehabbing from the Tommy John surgery he underwent in October 2024, but he should be good to go for the start of 2026 given that he was throwing multi-inning bullpen sessions late last season. The veteran right-hander has a 3.25 ERA, 1.12 WHIP and 9.6 K/9 since the start of the 2020 campaign, but there are major question marks regarding his durability as he enters his age-33 season. Musgrove made just 36 starts across 2023 and 2024 due to injuries (even before the Tommy John injury), and he's now coming off a lost season and major elbow surgery. Regaining his strong form in the first year back wouldn't be unheard of, but Musgrove's additional injury issues add another layer to consider. His ceiling is that of a top-end starter, but the floor here is zero.

Numerous factors have worked against Lawlar getting an extended chance in Arizona, from Eugenio Suarez’s handling third base in 2024, to Lawlar’s thumb surgery last spring, to his own need to find another defensive position. A onetime top-10 overall prospect, Lawlar will experiment in the outfield in the hopes the Diamondbacks can jump start his career. He hit .313/.403/.564 with 11 homers and 20 steals in 63 games for Triple-A Reno last season, and he’s still only 23 years old, so don’t forget about him as a prospective breakthrough candidate if he’s looking good during Cactus League play.

A 31-year-old journeyman, O'Brien added velocity to his sinker and spin to his slider and broke through for the 2025 Cardinals, ultimately earning himself their closer job in the month of September. That might give him a leg up in their spring competition for the role, and his ground ball leaning and ability to suppress hard contact does minimize the downside if he emerges. Monitor O'Brien's spring progress, which will ultimately decide whether holds or saves are his target, but there's enough opportunity here to make him a viable fantasy late-rounder.

One of four players in history with four 50-homer seasons, and one of three to hit 50-plus homers while winning the batting title (Jimmie Foxx, 1938; Mickey Mantle, 1956), Judge is baseball's preeminent all-around hitter. He has claimed three of the past four AL MVP awards, covering a span during which he hit .311 with an average of 53 home runs, 116 RBI, 118 runs scored and 114 walks per year. Now 33, Judge has also sufficiently answered the injury question that plagued him earlier in his career, as he has appeared in at least 152 games in three of the past four years, while batting .305/.473/.634 with 16 homers across his final 49 regular-season contests following a 10-day IL stint for an elbow issue in July/August. He's an exemplary choice to begin your draft in any fantasy format.

Kurtz ascended to the majors just one month into the 2025 season, ready to deliver one of the most impressive power displays we've ever seen from a rookie. His 36 home runs were 10th-most in history by a rookie, his 173 OPS+ was second-best in the modern era (minimum 450 plate appearances) and his .329 isolated power was second to only Aaron Judge's .343 in 2017. In fact, Kurtz and Judge are the only players in the 11 Statcast seasons to register at least 15% Barrel and 50% hard-hit rates as rookies (again, 450-PA minimum). That Kurtz only improved as the season progressed eases the worry of any sophomore slump, and he'll still call HR-friendly Sutter Health Park his home in 2026. While history cautions against players repeating the kind of debut that Kurtz just had, he's one of the rare young sluggers with a chance to do it, making him a strong early-round selection.

Alvarez's 2025 was an injury nightmare, from the hand injury he suffered in April -- initially diagnosed as a sprain but ultimately discovered to be a small fracture -- to the season-ending ankle sprain he suffered in September, just 19 games into his return from the prior ailment. It unfortunately continued a pattern of health questions for the Astros slugger who, when healthy, has consistently proven himself to be one of the best all-around hitters in the game. From 2021-24, Alvarez ranked third in OPS (.946) and hard-hit rate (53.8%) and seventh in batting average (.294). Bear in mind that during those 19 late-season, healthy games, he posted significantly better numbers in all three of those categories. A healthy spring training would go a long way towards easing prospective fantasy managers' nerves with this extreme risk/reward pick, but he's far too talented to let slip much further than the first 20 or so picks of any draft.

Freeman is aging like a fine California wine even if he is no longer playing every single game in a season. His days of 100-plus runs and 100-plus RBI appear to be over as his power is waning in his mid-30s, but he is still one of the few five-category producers at his position. He was able to hit .295 last year despite his strikeout rate surging to its highest level since his 2016 season after a long trend of Freeman having one of the better rates in the league. Ideally, Freeman would get some half days at DH, but that is not an option on the Dodgers. Instead, he gets to enjoy hitting behind Shohei Ohtani and Mookie Betts and in front of Will Smith, Max Muncy and Tesocar Hernandez. His 2024-2025 production is very repeatable with his skills and lineup spot, but don't get greedy.

Fried settled in nicely in his first year in pinstripes, setting personal bests in wins (19), starts (32), innings pitched (195 1/3) and strikeouts (189). He performed consistently excellent outside of an eight-start, July/early August stretch in which his control wavered (6.80 ERA, 8.3 BB%). These days, that's the description of a fantasy ace, as few pitchers are spared the occasional wart, and most have similar, minor injury questions to what's in Fried's past. He's one of the higher-floor options at the position, and one of the few pitchers who, health willing, seems likely to exceed the 200-IP threshold. Build your staff around him with confidence.

One of the best control specialists in baseball, Kirby's 2025 was sidetracked by shoulder inflammation that cost him most of spring training and nearly two regular-season months. He'd rebound with 11 quality starts, a 3.59 ERA and 4.95 K/BB ratio over his final 17 starts -- and he was productive in three of his four postseason starts. All of this offers encouragement for a 2026 rebound. Kirby's 3.6% walk rate over his first four MLB seasons is the second lowest by any pitcher in the modern era, and he has an underrated slider that's capable of generating strikeouts. There's risk here, but the prospective reward would easily place him among his position's top 10 performers.

Oblique issues sent Langford to the IL on three separate occasions in 2025, obstructing what was otherwise a solid step forward by him in his sophomore season. He was one of 16 players with at least 22 home runs and stolen bases, and he reflected noticeable gains in terms of Statcast Barrel and hard-hit rates, while finishing in the 85th percentile in line-drive rate. Now 24, Langford could be ready to come into his own, though better luck in the health department will certainly play a part. He's an early-to-mid round pick with upside in all formats.

Known as a great player with a spotty health history, Seager fell short of 125 games played for the third consecutive regular season, landing at just 102 games with the Rangers in 2025. The shortstop made multiple trips to the injured list early with a hamstring strain and missed the final month following an appendectomy. Even so, he reached 20 homers for the fourth consecutive campaign and for the sixth time in his career, having smacked 30-plus each of the three seasons prior to last. Seager has lost a bit off his batting average in recent years, as his numbers against lefties are in decline, but he still crushes right-handed pitching when available. Steals are not part of the equation and players don't typically get healthier in their 30s, but the five-time All-Star still offers a high upside if he can somehow stay on the field.

A Will Smith won another World Series, but Smith is more than just a funny trivia question. He has been a force at the catching position for fantasy managers these past few seasons, even as he lost some of the volume this past year as the designated hitter spot on the roster was re-occupied by Shohei Ohtani. Smith was on pace to best his 2024 production despite the reduction in plate appearances and also went on to post a career-best batting average in 2025. If anything, one could argue the reduced volume was a good thing for Smith to keep him fresh over the course of a full season under the physical demands of catching. This season should be more of the same for playing time and production with a step back toward his career level for batting average with batted-ball luck coming back to previous norms.

Injuries derailed King's 2025, from the shoulder inflammation that cost him nine weeks around midseason, to the left knee inflammation that cost him one month just one start into his return from the former ailment. His raw stuff suffered accordingly (and predictably), though the winter's rest and a strong Cactus League showing could restore his potential as one of the position's top 20. When at his best, King has four offerings that generate at least a 25% whiff rate (four-seamer, changeup, sweeper and slider), and he's one of the better pitchers at suppressing hard contact. Let his March drive your draft decision, but he's at least a worthwhile risk/reward middle rounder.

Castillo has outpitched his peripherals since joining the Mariners in 2022, and it may be by design rather than just good fortune. With the Reds, Castillo was an extreme groundball pitcher which helped offset the homer-friendly Great American Ball Park. In the Pacific Northwest, he is leaning more on his four-seam fastball, which generates more flyballs. T-Mobile Park suppresses home runs, so while his home-run rate has risen, it remains reasonable, and the added flyballs are driving a BABIP between .267 and .285 over the past four seasons. The change in approach has sent his strikeout rate into freefall, denting his fantasy allure and increasing his dependence on a low BABIP, a slippery slope. Entering his age-33 season, Castillo's floor is more wobbly than usual, and without strikeouts, the ceiling is limited.

Although a back issue cost him the first month-plus of 2025, Suarez swiftly recaptured his prior form as one of the game's best command artists, as for the fifth consecutive season he placed in at least the 70th percentile in terms of average exit velocity and hard-hit rate allowed. In fact, he tied for the season's longest consecutive quality start streak (10, May 10-June 29). These things appealed to the Red Sox, who, despite an overstuffed rotation, brought him on as a reliable, middle-of-the-staff innings eater. Fantasy managers should regard him the same way, understanding that such pitchers typically carry a little more value in points than rotisserie leagues.

Kwan could not sustain the power gains from the prior season, though he still reached double-digit home runs for the second straight year. The 2024 spike was driven by more flyballs, and while he elevated the ball even more last season, the contact quality was not as strong, resulting in fewer homers and a career-low BABIP. Only three qualified hitters put the ball in play more often, keeping Kwan a steady batting average contributor, and he matched his career high with 21 steals. His durability also returned, as he missed just six games after appearing in only 122 the year before. Ignore the dip in power and draft Kwan for average and speed, with any home runs coming as a bonus.

Stewart is an MLB-ready hitter with growing power who merely needs a defensive place to play. He hit five homers across an 18-game "cup of coffee" with the Reds, playing more at first base than at third, but he'll probably be in the spring mix at both spots due to the team's injury question marks at those positions, although Eugenio Suarez's addition hurt his chances for everyday at-bats. Stewart hit .309/.383/.524 with 20 homers and 17 steals in 118 games between Double-A Chattanooga and Triple-A Louisville last season, and he'll have the Reds' homer-friendly ballpark helping his cause. He's a late-round flier in redrafts as is, and a solid dynasty building block as well.

Baseball's top-scoring fantasy pitcher over the first four seasons of his Yankees career (2020-23), Cole missed the first three months of 2024 due to an elbow injury, then ultimately succumbed to 2025-ending Tommy John surgery last March. A 14-month recovery timetable would have him ready to rejoin the big-league club in May, though the variability of return date and initial performance level coming off that operation lends uncertainty to his 2026 draft stock. Cole will be one of the most important pitchers to track once he resumes game competition (exhibition or minor-league level) in the spring, but his skill set makes him one of the best IL stashes for prospective front-of-a-staff fantasy production in the season's second half (or even its final four months).

McGonigle hit .305/.408/.583 in 88 games across three minor-league levels last season, walking 13 more times than he struck out, while hitting 19 homers and stealing 10 bases. He's perhaps the most well-rounded prospect among those with a likely 2026 ETA, and the Tigers have the option of breaking him in at either second base or shortstop once he's ready. McGonigle's skill set is great for all fantasy play, but he's looking like a prospective points-league gem. Consider him a dynasty building block and a �must get� in redrafts the moment he's promoted.

One of baseball's best bat handlers -- he's one of four players with at least 85% contact and 27.5% line-drive rates and 500 plate appearances over the last two seasons combined -- Donovan's skill set makes him one of the most underrated points-league players, even if he's only a back-of-your-roster utility type in rotisserie formats. Traded to the Mariners in February, he’ll likely serve as their leadoff man against right-handed pitchers, giving him more of a matchup lean in shallow mixed leagues but also boosting his run-scoring potential on the whole. Donovan's ceiling isn't especially high, but he's likely to deliver another top-100 fantasy point total in 2026.

The Tigers opened the season without a defined closer, and Vest was not part of the early mix. After posting a 1.17 ERA and 0.52 WHIP with nine strikeouts in 7.2 innings, however, he earned the first of what became a team-leading 23 saves. Manager A.J. Hinch leaned most heavily on Vest while still playing matchups, which allowed him to add four holds. Illustrating reliever ERA volatility, Vest logged his highest ERA since 2022, even as his xFIP and SIERA were their lowest over that span. He is not as overpowering as the top-tier closers, but he fanned more than a batter per inning over the past three seasons. Detroit bolstered their bullpen with fellow right-handers Kenley Jansen and Kyle Finnegan, yet Hinch remains noncommittal on roles. Vest fits well in leagues that count holds, as he should continue to work in high-leverage spots regardless.

Teel, the primary piece in the December 2024 Garrett Crochet trade, brought his intriguing combination of plate discipline, pop and smarts on the basepaths to the south side of Chicago beginning last June, putting forth one of the better beneath-the-radar campaigns among rookies. Among those with at least 250 plate appearances, his .375 OBP ranked third and his .349 wOBA sixth. From his debut date forward, he had the 12th-most fantasy points among catcher-eligibles of any experience level (140). Teel figures to again rotate with fellow youngster Edgar Quero between catcher and DH, though it's important to note that he's the more integral piece in the team's future plans. Teel could be ready for a big step forward in 2026, making him a catcher with upside to target if you're going the cheap route at the position.

Carroll rebounded from a disappointing sophomore 2024 -- one in part caused by tweaks he made to his swing the preceding winter that threw off his rhythm -- to register a 30/30 season for the first time in his career. He has now exceeded 400 fantasy points in each of his three complete MLB years, testament to his extra-base ability with the bat and selectivity at the plate. Carroll's .282 isolated power was exceeded by only six other qualified hitters, and he set a personal best with both his fly-ball and Statcast Barrel rates. He'll play 2026 at a prime-age 25, but a broken hamate bone in February cast doubt upon his availability for Opening Day and might require some time to recapture his timing thereafter. Carroll is still capable of first-round fantasy production, but keep tabs on his recovery before spending one of the draft's very first picks on him.

One of baseball's best power sources, Schwarber joins Aaron Judge and Shohei Ohtani as the only hitters with at least 180 home runs and 400 each of runs and RBI over the past four seasons, and his 18.3% Statcast Barrel rate in that time is fourth-best among qualifiers. Schwarber's keen eye at the plate, too, is an asset in points leagues, as his 426 total walks and 15.2% walk rate over that same span rank third and fourth. That he has also improved substantially against left-handed pitchers, posting his two best single-year OPS against them in the past two years, only helps cement his case as a foundational fantasy pick, even as a 33-year-old who can be slotted only at DH (UT).

Olson is a model of durability and elite power, even if his borderline MVP-candidate 2023 season now looks like an outlier. He hasn't missed a game since May 1, 2021, and is the only player with at least 29 home runs and .200 isolated power in each of the past seven full MLB seasons (2018-19, '21-25). As a heart-of-the-order hitter for a Braves lineup that feels like it has been stricken with exceedingly awful luck over the past two seasons, Olson seems a strong bet for another near-30 HR/100 RBI campaign, with the possibility of more power upside. He's worth selecting in the early rounds of any draft.

Gifted with a high-90s fastball, blossoming sweeper and some of the most pinpoint control of anyone in baseball, Woo broke through in a big way in 2025. He finished fifth among pitchers in fantasy points, third in WHIP and K/BB ratio, fourth in quality starts (21) and fifth in wins. Perhaps most importantly, he remained healthy for long enough to make a career-high 30 starts. A pectoral strain in September limited his contributions during the team's playoff run, but the winter's rest should afford him the chance to heal and merely warrants a quick glance once spring training opens. Woo is a legitimate fantasy ace.

For a pitcher to possess as stuff as filthy as Miller's is flat-out unfair. Among those who have thrown at least 400 of either pitch in any of the 18 seasons for which we have pitch data, Miller's 101.2-mph average fastball velocity last season was second highest, while his 54.6% whiff rate with his slider was 15th. Though his deadline deal to the Padres bumped him from his prior closer role, he thrived in setup relief with his new team, scoring the sixth-most fantasy points (124) despite not winning a game and posting only two saves in that time. Robert Suarez's winter departure paved the way for Miller to reclaim the ninth-inning role in San Diego, from which the right-hander has a wide-open path to being the top performing relief pitcher in fantasy baseball in 2026.

Between his having bulked up, made a batting-stance adjustment and adopted a torpedo bat during the prior winter, Rice's breakthrough last season had plenty of rationale. His hard-hit rate spiked by 20%, and he finished sixth among batting title-eligible hitters in expected wOBA. But perhaps most important for fantasy purposes, Rice put in enough time the plate to qualify at catcher, where his offensive contributions carry far more weight than at first base. Rice could again split time between the two positions, but consider that his 26 homers last season ranked fifth among catcher-eligibles for 2026. He's an up-and-comer well worth an early-round pick.

Two-pitch guys are supposed to be relievers and not starters, but Gausman never got that message as he continues to ride his heavy fastball-splitter approach to continued success as a major-league starter. Gausman's 2025 saw him work a career high in regular-season innings along with another 30 stressful postseason innings which might be a cause for concern heading into 2026 (see Zac Gallen from 2023 to 2024). Over the past five seasons, Gausman is one of just three pitchers with at least 1000 strikeouts and is tied for second in games started while also being second in innings pitched. Everything looks good for his skills, but workhorses eventually stop being workhorses, so proceed with a degree of caution.

Soderstrom got off to a scorching start in 2025. Through three weeks, he was the MLB leader in home runs and was fourth among hitters in fantasy points. He ultimately delivered a modest breakthrough campaign, despite the arrival of eventual Rookie of the Year Nick Kurtz shifting him to left field in late April. While Soderstrom couldn’t maintain that lofty pace, he maintained solid power numbers, held his own against left-handed pitchers and had better road numbers away from hitter-friendly Sutter Health Park than at home. He’ll need to add more loft to his swing to take another big step forward from here, but as a 24-year-old in a good home environment for bats, he’s well worth a mid-to-late round fantasy pick.

Perez's return from April 2024 Tommy John surgery offered far more promise in terms of his underlying metrics than what his surface numbers indicated. Among pitchers with at least as many as his 20 starts, he ranked second in average fastball velocity (97.9 mph), fifth in BAA (.195) and 15th in strikeout rate (27.3%). Perez also finished the year with a flourish, averaging 16.0 fantasy points over his final four starts, further underscoring his growth potential heading into 2026. Expect the Marlins to be cautious with their 22-year-old, soon-to-be-ace, but he's one of the best upside picks among starting pitchers.

Early in 2025, it again looked as though Harris's production would fall short of his skills and athleticism. He went into the All-Star break hitting .210/.234/.317, but then returned with an open stance and higher hand position and posted a .299/.315/.530 line the rest of the season. The changes more than doubled his barrel rate and lifted his hard-hit rate by nine points, placing him among the league's best in the second half. He cooled off in September, but the quality of his contact matched July and earlier levels, with August marking his best month by hard-hit rate. While his month-to-month splits raise questions about the true effect of the adjustments, the second-half surge has turned mounting frustration into tempered optimism.

Despite Woodruff recently missing the better part of two years and ending 2025 back on the injured list with a lat strain, Milwaukee extended him the qualifying offer for 2026, which speaks to just how well he pitched when available last season. After his recovery from 2023 shoulder surgery was set back several times, Woodruff finally returned with five quality starts in his first six outings before enduring a couple hiccups in August. His xBA and xERA were both among the very best in baseball in his limited sample of 64.2 big-league innings last season. The right-hander has always gotten whiffs and the Brewers have proven they know what they're doing in regards to pitching. Chasing a full season's worth of starts would be a fool's errand, but the team clearly has high hopes for Woodruff in regards to both performance and workload.

Lopez was mostly a high-average speed threat for the Marlins in 2024, but he added a bit more pop in 2025 at the expense of his batting average. He batted .246 in 143 games last season -- down from .270 -- and totaled 15 home runs and 15 steals, compared to six homers and 20 stolen bases over 161 fewer plate appearances in 2024. The improved power may not stick around since Lopez still didn't consistently make hard contact, but double-digit homers with 20-plus steals is a realistic expectation at this point, though the other counting stats are likely to be limited. Lopez opened 2025 as Miami's primary second baseman but was shifted to shortstop midseason, and his strong defense at both positions will help to keep him in the lineup.

Unable to maintain the elevated strikeout rate that earned him the Giants' closer role over the final two months of 2024, Walker was demoted back to middle relief after posting a 6.43 ERA over his first 16 appearances last season. He'd ultimately get another chance to close in August and September following the trade of Camilo Doval, but Walker's slider wasn't nearly as effective in 2025 as in the past, and he ultimately finished the season with MLB's fourth-most blown saves (7). Walker should begin 2026 as the team's primary ninth-inning option, with good enough command and a ground-ball leaning that would make him a useful mid-range fantasy option, but he'd need to make a significant adjustment in order to vault into the position's top 10.

Torres enjoyed a resurgent campaign in his first season with Detroit, making his first All-Star team since 2019, though he regressed hard in the second half with a .659 OPS compared to an .812 OPS before the break. After the Tigers were eliminated from the postseason, Torres underwent sports hernia surgery. He was cleared for full activity in December. Despite the late slide, the Tigers extended him the qualifying offer for 2026, which Torres accepted. With that, the 29-year-old will return to second base and presumably to the top third of the order after batting almost exclusively first or second under manager A.J. Hinch last season. While Torres does not pack the power or speed to be especially exciting for fantasy purposes, he does enough to be worthwhile in most formats.

Tovar was hampered by injuries for much of the first half of 2025 and ended up playing in just 94 games on the year, finishing with nine home runs, five steals, 33 RBI, 44 runs and a .253/.294/.400 slash line. That line was a bit worse across the board compared to 2024, with slugging percentage being the major drop since his homer total was nearly cut in third. Despite some inconsistency, Tovar posted career bests in strikeout and walk rates (25.1 percent and 5.5 percent, respectively). The Coors Field effect has definitely been in play with a home average of .339 compared to .172 on the road. Tovar has showcased a decent floor for a mid-tier shortstop and should be able to get back around 20 long balls and double-digit steals with a healthy campaign in 2026.

Kikuchi found another gear after being traded to the Astros at the 2024 deadline, largely by shaving half a tick off his curve and changeup, which made his fastball play up. That showing led the Angels to sign him to a long-term deal, banking on some carryover. Instead, all of his pitches lost velocity last season, whether by design or age-related decline. The reduced velocity aided his offspeed and breaking pitches but hurt his four-seamer, contributing to his lowest strikeout rate since 2019 and his highest walk rate in three years. At 35 years old, and with 97 starts over the past three seasons, Kikuchi faces a number of questions including whether the velocity returns. The left-hander can still contribute, but his best use comes at home in favorable matchups.

The epitome of a risk/reward player in fantasy baseball, Acuna's career has been highlighted by extreme highs, like his historic 42/75 campaign of 2023, and painful (literally) lows, such as the separate ACL surgeries he has had on each knee in 2021 (right) and 2024 (left). It makes him one tough cookie as far as estimating his draft stock, as he has missed more games over the past five seasons (305) than any player with even a prayer of going among the top-25 picks of any mixed-league draft. However, in Acuna's defense, he has made strides in improving his plate discipline, boosting his fantasy points league stock, over the past three seasons. His contact-quality metrics last year were outstanding and he should be more willing to be aggressive on the basepaths this season as he gets further removed from his most recent ACL operation. Predicting historical outcomes is fantasy folly, but in his age-28 season, Acuna might yet roar back with another stat line for the ages.

Chourio's first two MLB seasons were almost spot-on as far as counting numbers are concerned. Often, fantasy managers might therefore assume the player has locked in that level of performance expectation, but in his case, remember that Chourio will begin 2026 only 21 years, 15 days old, and he showed glimpses of growth in 2025. His postseason -- .341/.362/.682 rates and four home runs in 12 games, despite dealing with hamstring issues -- was as compelling evidence as any, but he also reflected noticeable jumps in his bat speed and Barrel rate. Besides, he seemed to be turning the corner in early July before the hamstring problem first began. Chourio still has a path to superstardom and, while he's a potentially more profitable pick in rotisserie than points leagues, he's a player you shouldn't let last more than a few rounds in any draft.

Through 15 starts, Sale was on track to defend his 2024 Cy Young, carrying a 2.52 ERA and 1.16 WHIP with 114 strikeouts across 89.1 innings before a fractured left ribcage sidelined him for a little more than 10 weeks. He returned without missing a beat, logging a 2.72 ERA and 0.83 WHIP over his final six starts and striking out 51 in 36.1 frames. On the season, the underlying skills remained elite, as his 26.1 strikeout-minus-walk percentage ranked fourth among pitchers with at least 120 innings. While the injury underscores the health risk attached to the left-hander entering his age-37 season, the fact that it was not arm-related has kept early drafters confident, with Sale still among the first 10 starters selected.

Webb has logged the most innings of any pitcher over the past five seasons, throwing 40 more innings than any other pitcher. Over those 968.1 innings, he has logged a 3.19 ERA, 1.16 WHIP and an 18 K-BB percentage. He took his production up a level in 2025 striking out 224 batters, besting his previous career high by 30, and he did so in fewer innings than he he needed to set that previous personal record. Webb was once primarily a sinker-slider-changeup pitcher, but has also recently introduced a cutter and four-seamer to his repertoire and now both lefties and righties have to discern between five different offerings.  He is one of five pitchers to win at least 10 games in each of the past five seasons and there is little reason to think he will fall short of hitting his usual benchmarks in 2026.

Better injury luck and some slight elevation in his launch angle fueled a major breakthrough for Pasquantino last season, as he became the first left handed-hitting Royal with a 30-HR, 100-RBI campaign since George Brett 40 years earlier. While Pasquantino's underlying contact-quality metrics hinted some good fortune was involved -- his Barrel and hard-hit rates placed in the 65th and 57th percentiles -- his prospects for a repeat were helped by the Royals' January announcement that they'll shrink Kauffman Stadium's power-alley dimensions for 2026. He's a prime-age first baseman with elite contact skills and should be targeted in the early-to-mid rounds of any draft.

One of 2025's most unexpected breakthrough performers, Perdomo joined Shohei Ohtani and Bobby Witt Jr. as the only players with at least a .275 batting average, 20 home runs, 20 stolen bases and a 7.0 WAR. Everything clicked for Perdomo, from the counting numbers-inflating 129 starts he made out of the top three spots in the lineup, to the 8.4% HR/FB rate that was more than double his MLB career number entering the year, though those are two areas now subject to some regression. His contact-skills growth represented the bigger story, elevating his floor and making him an ideal points-league pick. So long as you're not expecting a repeat of his 20 homers or 100 RBI, he should be a fine early-to-mid-round pick.

After finishing third in the majors in stolen bases in 2024, effectively a two-category player (steals and runs), Garcia went all Willie Mays Hayes-in-�Major League 2� last season, inexplicably trading his speed in the quest for power. He attempted only one stolen base across his final 44 games and just five over his final 79, while more than doubling his home run total for the full season. That's not to knock Garcia's improvements as he made huge strides with his selectivity and contact and saw a decent bump in terms of contact quality. We'd, of course, prefer to see him capitalize upon his career best .351 OBP with bushels of steals, which would make him more of an early-round target in rotisserie leagues. As is, he's a solid mid-round pick as he enters his age-26 season.

Bednar's overall 2025 numbers were so good that you almost forget he was sent to Triple-A early in the season because he got off to such an awful start. Bednar had a rough spring and then blew two of his first three save chances opening weekend with some bad command and worse batted-ball luck which led Pittsburgh to send him to Indianapolis for some fine-tuning. Bednar returned three weeks later and was utterly dominant as a closer, winning six games and saving 26 more while striking out 83 batters and limited opposing hitters to a .183 average in his time between the Pirates and Yankees. Whereas he was a fringe top closer option heading into 2025, he is now a firm first-closer option in 2026 with the Yankees fully confident in Bednar's abilities as evidenced by them letting Devin Williams and Luke Weaver depart in free agency.

Ramirez arrived in Miami three weeks into the season and, as is all the rage these days, saw near-everyday time between catcher and DH to fuel what was the third-most fantasy points by any catcher-eligible player from that point forward. Though he cooled over the season's final three months, batting only .212 with a .633 OPS, his fantasy value was buoyed by his 15 stolen bases over that time. His well-rounded game, and his penchant for contact, gives him a good shot at another top-10 catcher season, if not a step forward in 2026.

Misiorowski, one of the game's top prospects, arrived in the majors last June to pitch five no-hit innings in his first career start, and post a 2.81 ERA and 33.7% strikeout rate across his first five. Unfortunately, between his mediocre control and the shin contusion that cost him a 17-day stay on the IL, he couldn't maintain that pace the rest of the way and his ERA ballooned to 5.36 across his final nine starts and one relief appearance. Misiorowski's raw stuff, however, was consistently excellent, and if the Brewers trust him to pitch deeper into games, he could break out in a big way in 2026. There's danger here of overrating him, but among mid-round picks, he carries a lot of upside.

Handed the Brewers' closer role at the onset of last season following the trade of Devin Williams, Megill upped both his fastball velocity and strikeout rate to score the eighth-most fantasy points among relief pitchers through late August, when he was lost for a month due to a flexor strain. Megill would return in time for the Brewers' playoff run, although Abner Uribe's performance in the interim thrusts the position into somewhat of a spring competition entering 2026. Megill figures to be the favorite to close, with similar top-10 positional production after his back-to-back elite campaigns, though this is a situation to watch throughout March.

The Cardinals moved Contreras from catcher to first base last offseason, but the defensive move didn't bring significant change at the plate as he posted a .257/.344/.447 slash line with 20 home runs, 80 RBI and 70 runs in 135 games. A .791 OPS ended up being his worst mark since 2021, and that was largely fueled by his 8.2 percent walk rate, which was nearly five points worse than his 2024 mark. Being traded from the rebuilding Cardinals to the Red Sox in December should provide Contreras with the potential for more run production in 2026, especially since Fenway Park is more hitter friendly to right-handed bats than Busch Stadium. Contreras has a pretty well established floor with an average of 20 home runs, 59 RBI, 60 runs and a .252 batting average across the past five seasons, so he's a fairly safe mid-tier fantasy target.

McKinstry is a sneaky late-round pick in deeper mixed leagues, particularly those that use roto scoring, thanks to his positional flexibility -- he qualifies at three different spots -- and stolen base contributions. He has swiped at least 16 bases in each of the last three seasons and had 46 extra-base hits in 2025, while registering personal bests in most offensive categories. McKinstry’s contact quality remains only mediocre, however, and his statistical profile lacks much in the way of matchups he can exploit. Regard him as a back-of-your-roster type, but not a player likely to make many advances in 2026.

Dingler took over as Detroit's primary backstop in 2025 and delivered a quality rookie campaign, finishing the regular season with 13 homers, 57 RBI, 54 runs and a .278/.327/.425 slash line in 126 games. Previous No. 1 catcher Jake Rogers is coming off a second straight disappointing season at the plate, so he's likely to stick in the backup job to begin 2026. Dingler didn't walk much with just 23 free passes but had a 23.5 percent strikeout rate. Dingler also provided strong defensive value behind the plate, which will be key to maintaining playing time at a premium defensive position, though he may not quite be ready to truly play every day like the top catchers in baseball. Repeating a strong average with 10-15 homers and modest counting stats is a fair expectation in 2026.

O’Hearn has carved out a “strong side of a straight platoon” role over the past three seasons, batting .280/.346/.445 against righties in that time, which makes him one of the more useful late-round picks in fantasy leagues that allow daily transactions. His move to Pittsburgh, and pitcher-friendly PNC Park, does lower his prospective number of actionable matchups somewhat, but he’s someone to keep in mind as you round out your roster.

After a year away from the 30/30 club, �J-Rod� roared back to that status in 2025, with a campaign that showed relevant growth for points league managers. Rodriguez set a personal best with his 71.8% contact rate, which spiked to 77.4% over the final two months, during which time he hit .299. Between that and the gradual lowering of his ground ball rate from August forward, he could be primed for even bigger things -- perhaps a five-category monster year, or at least a boost in home runs -- as he enters his age-25 season. Rodriguez is a clear first-round talent in rotisserie leagues, but he's also a building-block player in points leagues.

In two seasons since shifting from relief to the rotation, Crochet has handled the move with aplomb. His 2025 reflected significant gains, not only in the 59 1/3 additional innings he tallied, but also the near-run he shaved off his ERA as well as his doubling his number of quality starts (22) relative to 2024. Crochet also gained velocity over the course of the summer, a signal that he has now settled into his role as a staff ace. He was a model of consistency, the only pitcher to score as many as 73 fantasy points in each of the season's six months. He's an ideal pitcher around whom to build your team, and a first-round pick in points leagues.

Baseball's consensus top prospect at the time of his June 2025 debut, Anthony put forth a promising, albeit far from eye-popping, three months of production before an oblique strain brought his year to a premature close. During that time, he managed the majors' second-best Statcast hard hit rate (60.4%) and eighth-best OBP (.396), though he put the ball on the ground too often (50.6% rate). The seeds are there for Anthony to swiftly develop into a fantasy superstar, though the progression is as likely to be gradual than all at once in 2026. So long as the cost doesn't require a guarantee of the latter, he's one of the best upside picks in the early-to-mid rounds of your draft.

A shining star at one of the game's thinner positions, Marte has hit at least 25 home runs with an .800 OPS in each of the last three seasons. No other second baseman can claim more than one year of either number. Marte has done it with a combination of elite plate discipline, raw power and contact. In 2025, he put forth his best season from the left side of the plate (.288/.377/.519 rates) since 2019, addressing one of the few previously ordinary facets of his game. The only knocks on Marte now are questions about an eventual career downslope, as he'll play 2026 at age 32, and his injury history, as he has missed at least 25 games in four of the past five seasons. They're minor questions, however, and drafting him as a foundational part of your fantasy team should pay big dividends from a tough-to-fill lineup spot.

From a rates perspective, Diaz's 2025 was up there alongside any of his best statistical seasons, including his outrageous, 57-save 2018. The main drawback was his garnering only 31 save chances -- an inexplicably low total for a closer from an 83-win team. Diaz departed the Mets during the winter for a Dodgers team that has finished second in the majors in save chances in both of the last two seasons, despite their never truly having a singular ninth-inning choice over that time. While manager Dave Roberts could exploit a matchup every now and then, Diaz's contract and raw stuff almost assuredly will earn him the role for 2026, from which the right-hander is as good a bet to top his position in fantasy value as anyone.

After two seasons of his elite velocity and swing-and-miss skills toiling in a closer's timeshare in manager Scott Servais' matchups-oriented bullpen, Munoz thrived as the Mariners' full-time guy in Dan Wilson's first full season calling the shots. Munoz finished second in fantasy points among relief pitchers, third in saves and fourth in ERA, not to mention he added 8 1/3 shutout innings and two saves in the Mariners' two-round playoff run. He'll return in the same role, for a similarly competitive team, meaning another run as a top-five fantasy closer seems likely.

Pena put together his first career All-Star season at 27 years old, hitting .304 with 17 homers and 20 steals across 125 games with the Astros, but injuries derailed him late. The shortstop missed the entire month of July with a fractured rib after being hit by a pitch and ended the season on the IL with an oblique injury. The biggest area of growth was in the BA department as he finished top five in MLB, though Statcast puts him at a .273 xBA based on the quality and amount of contact. Assuming full health after an offseason of rest, Pena will return to an everyday role in Houston where he has genuinely moved the needle since breaking in a few years back. Regression to the rate numbers seems likely, but it's reasonable to think Pena could still find another level with his counting stats in 2026.

A hot start to Cruz's 2025 -- he had eight homers and 14 stolen bases through his first 30 games -- seemed to signal the arrival of his long-anticipated breakthrough. However, over time, his former weaknesses continued to squeak through. He posted the third-worst contact rate (66.0%) and 16th-lowest launch angle (8.1 degrees) among batting title-eligibles, capping his power upside. He also hit an abysmal .102/.224/.176 against lefties, rendering him more of a matchups type. Now 27, Cruz still has time to patch those flaws in his game, but he's shaping up as more of a rotisserie-minded breakthrough candidate than a complete, all-around star. Think carefully before reaching for him in points-league drafts.

Heralded for his defense at third base, Chapman does not hit for a high batting average (career .240) but has been above a .750 OPS in all but one of his nine big-league seasons to date. Chapman has been a consistent contributor with 20-plus homers four of the past five years, reaching 21 with the Giants last season despite multiple trips to the IL with a hand injury he first suffered while diving back into the first-base bag in June. Chapman has added steals in the years since MLB limited the number of throws to first base among other rule changes to facilitate the running game, and he's now well established as a net positive on both sides of the ball. The two-time Platinum Glover projects to continue batting fourth or fifth on a daily basis for San Francisco, health permitting.

Abreu joined the Triple-Digit Club for the third straight season, reaching 100 strikeouts yet again, with only Cade Smith and Mason Miller achieving the milestone twice over that span. Abreu spent most of the season setting up Josh Hader, recording 25 holds, but he was pressed into closing in mid-August and delivered seven saves in eight chances. Curiously, he posted a 4.24 ERA and 1.53 WHIP during that stretch, but it was fueled by an uncharacteristically high .442 BABIP, over 60 points higher than the mark he posted the previous two seasons. It is not clear if Hader will be ready to start the season, which will drive up Abreu's price. Abreu sits atop the list of closers-in-waiting with the ability to protect ratios while contributing to strikeouts.

Suarez is coming off back-to-back top-10 fantasy closer seasons, his 76 saves during that time being MLB's most. However, let's address the elephant in the room following his departure from San Diego. He has an ERA nearly a full run higher away from Petco Park (3.41) than at it (2.44) for his career, with his other ratios reflecting a steep home/road split. Fortunately, Suarez's combination of high-90s average fastball velocity, elite control and balanced platoon splits should afford him a relatively soft landing in Atlanta's Truist Park -- a more hitter-friendly, but hardly heavenly, venue. Expect his ratios to rise, but as the Braves' clear closer, he should put forth another potential top-10 fantasy season at the position.

No other active closer has more saves than Hader over the past five seasons. His 28.8 strikeout-minus-walk percentage lead all closers in that time, as well. Throw in the fourth-best WHIP and the second-best batting average against, and you may ask yourself why there is any reason Hader is not the first closer off the board in fantasy drafts. The answer to that question lies in the uncertainty surrounding his health, as he came down with shoulder soreness in early August and never returned to the mound, then dealt with biceps inflammation at the onset of spring training. It is also worth remembering that Hader was coming off a post-COVID high for workload from 2024 to 2025, which could help explain the injuries. Keep tabs on his progress as Opening Day approaches.

Apparently, the fastball velocity drop he experienced in his final year in Japan was no mirage, as Sasaki struggled early in that regard in his first taste of the U.S. game, posting a 4.72 ERA and 15.6% strikeout and 14.3% walk rates in eight starts before a shoulder issue cost him the next three months. He'd return with elevated velocity and filthy stuff out of the bullpen in September and the playoffs, even handling some save chances in October, which offered a glimpse of his elite potential. Sasaki should be stretched out again to start this spring and, if he's looking similarly good -- monitor that velocity, which needs to be closer to 98 than 96 mph -- he'd be a breakout candidate, albeit one who might face an innings cap.

Burleson cut his chase rate down and saw immediate results in 2025, slashing .290/.343/.459 across 139 games with the Cardinals to win the Silver Slugger at the utility spot. He improved against lefties and led the team in OPS on the strength of improved patience and selectivity, though he ended up falling short of his 2024 totals in home runs, runs, RBI and steals due to missing time in the second half with a wrist injury. With Willson Contreras now in Boston, Burleson will take over as the everyday first baseman in St. Louis after splitting time between the outfield (74 games), first base (50 games) and DH (22 games) last season. The profile does not look out of place in the middle of a major-league lineup, and entering his age-27 campaign, Burleson still appears capable of more.

Seemingly blocked at his primary position at the MLB  level by Adley Rutschman, Basallo parlayed .270/.377/.589 rates and 23 homers in 76 games for Triple-A Norfolk into his first opportunity with the Orioles once Rutschman's oblique issues resurfaced in mid-August. Basallo would struggle through a too-aggressive approach at the plate, batting only .165 while striking out over 25% of the time, but he flashed decent pop and was a plenty serviceable backstop. He's expected to serve in a catcher/DH partnership with Rutschman in 2026, from which both will hinder the other's playing time somewhat, but also from which both could be fantasy-relevant and even prospective top-10 positional values. The long-term sky's the limit with this kid.

Bogaerts has been on a rather bizarre run in recent years with almost impossibly low counting stats for an established player of his caliber. A four-time All-Star and twice a 100-RBI bat during his time with the Red Sox, he has not reached even 60 RBI in a season with the Padres. Bogaerts missed time in 2024 with a fractured left shoulder and has now settled at exactly 11 homers in consecutive seasons. After transitioning to second base in 2024, Bogaerts moved back to shortstop in 2025, and with that he loses the dual eligibility that boosted his fantasy utility. The age-related decline began earlier for Bogaerts than most, but at 33 he is still a plus player for San Diego and the stolen bases help his case for continued mid-round interest.

One of baseball's most consistent, well-rounded players, Ramirez is one of only two with at least 20 home runs and 20 stolen bases in each of the past five seasons, averaging 31.6 and 32.0 over that time. He's also one of only four with at least a batting title-qualified 80% contact rate in all of those years. From a fantasy point-scoring perspective, he has finished top 10 among hitters in each of the past six seasons, which is twice as long as the players with the next-longest such streaks (3, by Shohei Ohtani and Juan Soto). Ramirez's 33 years of age raise slight concerns that his decline phase could soon gradually begin, but for 2026, at least, his five-tool ability makes him one of the top picks in any fantasy format.

Turner had back-to-back healthy seasons in 2022 and 2023, but he has hit the injured list both of the two past years, with a hamstring injury at fault in 2025. Turner was still eighth overall in stolen bases despite the hamstring injury, and he remains one of the fastest players in baseball. On some teams, Turner would run every time he reached base, but he also hits in front of Kyle Schwarber and the Phillies do not frequently wish to open up first base and instead rely upon the threat of the steal to help Schwarber see more fastballs. Turner would have scored 100-plus runs had he avoided the injury and is likely thrilled Schwarber is returning to the club. The injury risk is the only thing holding Turner back from being a first-round pick.

After setting the Mets' franchise record for home runs in what was the most well-rounded season of his seven-year MLB career, Alonso exercised his opt-out clause to take his wares to Baltimore. There, he'll get to play in a Camden Yards that played much more HR-friendly last season after the team moved the left field fence back in, which presents a good match for a player who just set personal bests in Statcast Barrel and hard-hit rates and average exit velocity. Now 31, Alonso has yet to show any signs of the aging curve taking hold, meaning he remains a top fantasy first baseman well worth a selection in the early-to-mid rounds.

Blame injuries, rather than the much-theorized �sophomore slump,� for what ailed Merrill in 2025. A hamstring strain in April, a concussion in June and an ankle sprain in August cost him a combined 44 games and three IL stints, between which he struggled to garner any sort of momentum. It ultimately caused him to attempt zero stolen bases after June 14. Despite this, Merrill sported similarly strong contact-quality metrics to those of his rookie 2024, and he finished the year with a flourish, batting .275/.320/.626 with seven homers and 16 RBI over his final 24 games. Here's hoping that it was a one-year aberration rather than the start of an injury-prone reputation, but Merrill has a lot of rebound potential among players you'll find in the early-to-middle stages of your draft.

Among the most shocking outcomes in fantasy baseball history has to be Naylor's 30 stolen bases last season, in a year where his Statcast sprint speed placed in the 3rd percentile -- third!!! Kudos to a guy who has one of the better success rates among base stealers historically, and is never afraid to run, but his 19 steals across 54 games once he was traded to Dan Wilson's Mariners is simply unsustainable (even though Wilson is one of the game's most aggressive managers on that front). And all this overshadows what are pretty good hitting metrics and balanced platoon splits, meaning Naylor is in about as good a place for a 20/20 potential season as he could ask. He's an underrated, early-round potential pick in rotisserie leagues, and is an early-to-mid rounder in points leagues.

After a massive rookie breakthrough in middle relief in 2024, Smith graduated to closer status last August, going 13-for-16 converting his saves with a 2.60 ERA and 39 K's compared to two walks over the season's final two months. Considering he was fantasy baseball's top point scorer among relievers during that time (162 points), there's every reason to believe he can contend for that status working in the role full-time in 2026. Smith has been especially dominant against left-handed hitters (.162/.218/.270 rates in his two MLB seasons), and he made big strides in minimizing hard contact last year -- a combination that makes him one of the safest investments at his position despite his limited closer experience.

The Cubs entered the season with an organizational focus on pulling more flyballs, and Suzuki set the tone by increasing his pull rate while maintaining an above-average flyball rate. The approach yielded new career highs with the Cubs in ISO and home runs. That power jump came with a 38-point drop in batting average, though his xBA was only three points lower than the prior season. His strikeout rate ticked down slightly but remained well above league average. Most notably, Suzuki appeared in 151 games, marking his first season since coming over in which he avoided the IL entirely. Often, a year after a major adjustment is used to recalibrate, but Suzuki would be best served sticking with the same approach and hoping his batting average moves closer to his expected mark.

Wheeler was amid one of the most remarkable five-year runs of any active pitcher at the time he succumbed to thoracic outlet surgery last September. Even missing the season's final six weeks, from 2021-25, he ranked first among pitchers in fantasy points (2,327), first in WHIP (1.00), tied for first in quality starts (99), second in strikeouts (1,041), third in ERA (2.90), tied for third in wins (65), fourth in innings pitched (908) and fifth in K/BB ratio (5.10). Wheeler's recovery timetable should place a return sometime around May 1, though there are risks involved with the speed and effectiveness of pitchers' rehabilitation, and his advancing age (35) raises an additional concern. He showed no ill effects of the aging process before the operation, however, so if you're willing to stash him in an IL spot hoping he makes a swift recovery, he still has an ace's fantasy ceiling.

Iglesias finished one save shy of his third straight 30-save season, largely due to early-season struggles that led to a temporary demotion from the closer role in early June. He carried a 6.75 ERA and 1.54 WHIP on June 5 after blowing his fourth save. Following five scoreless outings spanning four innings, with two holds and a win, Iglesias reclaimed primary closing duties. He then posted a 1.37 ERA and 0.69 WHIP the rest of the way, converting 21 of 22 save chances. While ERA swings are often variance-driven, Iglesias leaned more heavily on his four-seamer in the second half while nearly shelving his slider, which helped address the home-run issues from earlier in the season. Atlanta signed the veteran to a one-year, $16 million deal, ostensibly to close, but the team also added last year's saves leader, Robert Suarez.

"Well?! We're waiting!" It might feel like forever to fantasy managers, but it's important to remember that Holliday, the No. 1 pick of the 2022 Draft and consensus No. 1 prospect entering his 2024 MLB debut season, is still only 22 years old and just 427 professional games removed from high school. Not all prospects blossom immediately, and perhaps he's one of those who takes baby steps to get there. Holliday's metrics were so-so at best in his first full big-league campaign in 2025, but he did greatly improve his patience (95th percentile chase rate) and contact (80th percentile rate) during the season's second half, and he showed hints of future five-category rotisserie potential. That said, a fractured right hamate bone suffered in February will cost him important spring training time and likely land him on the IL to start the season. Holliday is still a high-upside middle-round pick, but picking him requires a bit of a leap of faith.

A plenty-productive fantasy closer for the Cardinals over the majority of the past two seasons -- his 610 points scored from the beginning of 2024 until his 2025 deadline trade were third-most among relief pitchers -- Helsley's numbers went right into the tank following his move into setup relief for the Mets. His prior control issues and difficulty minimizing hard contact came back to haunt him, as he had a 7.20 ERA in 22 games for his new team. Undeterred by this, the Orioles signed Helsley to a two-year deal to serve as their fill-in closer, a role from which his elite velocity and past experience should make him one of the better mid-round picks at the position.

Fairbanks remarkably avoided the injury bug in 2025 -- he had missed at least a month while on the IL in each of the previous four seasons -- and set personal bests with his 27 saves and 60 1/3 innings. While his raw stuff and underlying metrics, paled in comparison to his 2022-23 peak, he was plenty serviceable in the Rays' closer role. The Marlins, taking note of that and his 17 saves and 2.43 ERA away from homer-friendly George M. Steinbrenner Field, signed Fairbanks to handle their ninth inning, where he'll call a much more pitcher-friendly environment his home. Once the more durable, top-shelf relievers are off the board, this is a strong, risk/reward choice to fill out your pitching staff.

Williams took a sizable, statistical step forward in 2025, shaving more than a run and three-quarters off his ERA while reaching the 30-start plateau for the first time as a professional, but his skill set remained a bit of a mixed bag. He had the majors' worst qualified walk rate (11.8%), the widest negative ERA-FIP differential (-1.33) and poor metrics in terms of contact quality allowed, signaling regression coming due. Still, Williams is only 26 years old, equipped with a 96.6-mph fastball and a pair of elite breaking pitches (curveball, sweeper) that make him especially tough against lefties, giving him growth potential that could neutralize those luck factors. It's probably best to treat his draft stock similarly to his 2025 fantasy finishes: SP24 (points), SP28 (rotisserie).

Regarded as the Royals’ catcher of the future, or at least a catcher/DH partner for Salvador Perez until the latter’s retirement, Jensen has an unusually sound combination of plate discipline and pop -- or at least it’s unusual for a backstop. He received a September cup of coffee with the Royals, hitting three homers with a .941 OPS in his 20 games, and he now figures to grab a similar role with the big club to begin 2026. Jensen has one of the highest ceilings among young catchers, and the promise of DH at-bats boosts his appeal in the runs/RBI categories. If he looks likely to break camp with the team, he could be a top-10 fantasy catcher right from the start.

An elbow issue that required offseason surgery bumped Herrera off catcher and to DH around midseason, at a point in 2025 too early for him to log the requisite time to maintain eligibility behind the plate. It's a shame, as his skill set -- solid contact, plate discipline skills and pop, as well as aggressiveness on the bases -- is intriguing for fantasy purposes from a catcher, but much more commonplace from a DH (a position that lets you use anyone). The Cardinals claim that Herrera should be able to return to catching duties in 2026, but his defensive limitations there might slow that process. Considering he'd have a top-10 ceiling at catcher, take a flier on him late and keep your fingers crossed.
